Classic wrong turns: adding $u$ instead of subtracting it in the denominator; using $v-u$ for the approaching observer in (b); and forgetting that $u/v$ must be dimensionless (all speeds in the same units).

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.1 Range of a projectile on an inclined plane: the dependence on alpha and beta is through 2alpha - beta
questions.command_term: Show that, Hence, Find, Calculate, State
questions.question:
A ball is projected from a point $O$ on a plane inclined at an angle $\beta$ to the horizontal. The initial speed is $u$ and the initial direction makes an angle $\alpha$ with the horizontal, measured in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope. The ball moves up the plane. Air resistance is negligible.

Throughout this question take the axis parallel to the plane, pointing up the slope, and the axis perpendicular to the plane, pointing away from it.

(a)

Resolve the initial velocity and the acceleration due to gravity parallel and perpendicular to the plane, and hence show that the time of flight is

$$T = \frac{2u\sin(\alpha - \beta)}{g\cos\beta}.$$(The ball lands when its displacement perpendicular to the plane returns to zero.)

[4]

(b)

Hence show that the range $R$ measured up the plane is

$$R = \frac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}\left[\sin(2\alpha - \beta) - \sin\beta\right].$$

[4]

(c)

Hence find, in terms of $\beta$, the value of $\alpha$ that maximises $R$, and show that the maximum range is

$$R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g(1 + \sin\beta)}.$$

[4]

(d)

The ball is projected with $u = 30.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ up a plane with $\beta = 20.0^\circ$. Taking $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, calculate the maximum range up the plane and the corresponding value of $\alpha$.

A student suggests that the maximum range on any plane is obtained with $\alpha = 45^\circ$. Calculate the range this would give, and state by how much it falls short of the maximum.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Resolving the initial velocity: parallel to the plane $u\cos(\alpha - \beta)$, perpendicular to the plane $u\sin(\alpha - \beta)$ (A1). Resolving the acceleration due to gravity: parallel to the plane $g\sin\beta$ down the slope, perpendicular to the plane $g\cos\beta$ into the plane (A1). The perpendicular displacement returns to zero at landing, so with $s = u_\perp T - \tfrac{1}{2}a_\perp T^2$ (M1):
$$u\sin(\alpha - \beta)\,T - \tfrac{1}{2}g\cos\beta\,T^2 = 0,$$
and rejecting $T = 0$ gives $T = \dfrac{2u\sin(\alpha - \beta)}{g\cos\beta}$ (AG).

(b) Along the plane, $R = u\cos(\alpha - \beta)\,T - \tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\beta\,T^2$ (M1). Substituting $T$ from part (a) and writing the first term over the common denominator $g\cos^2\beta$ (M1):
$$R = \frac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}\left[2\sin(\alpha - \beta)\cos(\alpha - \beta)\cos\beta - 2\sin\beta\sin^2(\alpha - \beta)\right].$$
Using $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$ and $2\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos 2\theta$ with $\theta = \alpha - \beta$ (M1):
$$R = \frac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}\left[\sin(2\alpha - 2\beta)\cos\beta - \sin\beta\left(1 - \cos(2\alpha - 2\beta)\right)\right]$$
$$= \frac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}\left[\sin(2\alpha - 2\beta)\cos\beta + \sin\beta\cos(2\alpha - 2\beta) - \sin\beta\right].$$
The first two terms are the expansion of $\sin\left((2\alpha - 2\beta) + \beta\right) = \sin(2\alpha - \beta)$ (A1), giving the required result.

(c) The factor $\dfrac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}$ and the term $-\sin\beta$ are both independent of $\alpha$, so $R$ is a maximum when $\sin(2\alpha - \beta)$ is a maximum (M1), that is when $\sin(2\alpha - \beta) = 1$ and $2\alpha - \beta = 90^\circ$ (A1). Hence
$$\alpha = 45^\circ + \frac{\beta}{2}.$$
Then $R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}(1 - \sin\beta)$ (M1), and since $\cos^2\beta = 1 - \sin^2\beta = (1 - \sin\beta)(1 + \sin\beta)$,
$$R_{\max} = \frac{u^2(1 - \sin\beta)}{g(1 - \sin\beta)(1 + \sin\beta)} = \frac{u^2}{g(1 + \sin\beta)} \quad (\mathrm{AG}).$$
As a check, $\beta = 0$ gives $\alpha = 45^\circ$ and $R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$, the familiar flat-ground results.

(d) $\alpha = 45^\circ + \dfrac{20.0^\circ}{2} = 55.0^\circ$ (A1). Then
$$R_{\max} = \frac{30.0^2}{9.81(1 + \sin 20.0^\circ)} = \frac{900}{9.81 \times 1.3420} = 68.4\,\mathrm{m} \quad (\mathrm{A1}).$$
With $\alpha = 45^\circ$ instead, $\sin(2\alpha - \beta) = \sin(90^\circ - 20^\circ) = \sin 70^\circ$, so (M1)
$$R = \frac{900}{9.81\cos^2 20^\circ}\left[\sin 70^\circ - \sin 20^\circ\right] = \frac{900}{8.662}(0.9397 - 0.3420) = 62.1\,\mathrm{m} \quad (\mathrm{A1}),$$
which falls short of the maximum by $68.4 - 62.1 = 6.3\,\mathrm{m}$, about $9\,\%$ of the maximum range (A1). The student's rule is therefore correct only on level ground.
questions.explanation:
Everything hard about this item is in one line of part (b). Before the double-angle identity is applied, the range is a product of $\sin(\alpha - \beta)$ and $\cos(\alpha - \beta)$ plus a second term in $\sin^2(\alpha - \beta)$, and the dependence on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ runs through three separate places. After the identity, it runs through one: the whole of the $\alpha$-dependence is inside $\sin(2\alpha - \beta)$, and the maximum is read off by inspection. The identity is not a simplification for its own sake; it is what makes the optimisation possible at all.

The distractor is the flat-ground result. Every candidate knows that maximum range needs $45^\circ$, and the item is set up so that the obvious move is to carry that over unchanged. Part (d) makes the cost concrete: $6.3$ m out of $68.4$ m, about 9 per cent. That is a large enough gap to feel, and it is the kind of number that makes the general result memorable.

There is also a small structural point worth naming. The perpendicular axis is what determines the time of flight, and the parallel axis is what determines the range; keeping the two separate is what stops candidates from writing down a single SUVAT equation in the horizontal direction and hoping. Candidates who resolve along the horizontal and vertical instead can still reach the answer, but the algebra is considerably longer and the $\cos\beta$ in the denominator of $T$ is much easier to lose.

This is adapted from the Chinese Gaokao treatment of projectile motion on an inclined plane, where the result $\alpha = 45^\circ + \beta/2$ is a standard item in the mechanics repertoire. The Gaokao version typically asks only for the optimal angle. Here the derivation is scaffolded by two 'show that' parts so that the item sits at difficulty 4, and the final part quantifies the error in the flat-ground answer, which the source does not ask for.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.4 An Atwood machine with a massive pulley: the effective inertia is m1 + m2 + I/R^2
questions.command_term: State, Show that, Calculate, Determine, Explain
questions.question:
Two blocks of masses $m_1 = 4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2 = 2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ are connected by a light inextensible string that passes over a pulley. The pulley is a uniform disc of radius $R = 0.120\,\mathrm{m}$ and moment of inertia $I = 0.0180\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ about its axis. The string does not slip on the pulley, the axle is frictionless, and the blocks move vertically. Take $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

The block of mass $m_1$ is released from rest and moves downwards, so the block of mass $m_2$ moves upwards.

(a)

State, with a reason, why the tension in the string is not the same on the two sides of the pulley. Write an equation relating the two tensions to the angular acceleration of the pulley.

[3]

(b)

Show that the acceleration $a$ of the blocks is given by

$$a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2 + \dfrac{I}{R^2}}.$$

[4]

(c)

Calculate the acceleration of the blocks and the two tensions in the string. Verify that your values satisfy the rotational equation you wrote in part (a).

[4]

(d)

Determine the moment of inertia the pulley would need for the acceleration to be exactly half of what it would be if the pulley were massless. Express your answer both as the equivalent mass $I/R^2$ and as a moment of inertia in $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The pulley has moment of inertia, so a resultant torque is needed to give it an angular acceleration (A1). If the tensions were equal, the torques they exert about the axle would cancel exactly and the pulley could not accelerate, while the blocks would be accelerating -- which would mean the string was slipping (A1). Hence $T_1 > T_2$, and with $\tau = I\alpha$ and $a = \alpha R$:
$$ (T_1 - T_2)R = I\alpha = \frac{Ia}{R} \quad (\mathrm{A1}). $$

(b) For $m_1$ moving downwards: $m_1g - T_1 = m_1a$ (A1). For $m_2$ moving upwards: $T_2 - m_2g = m_2a$ (A1). Adding these and using the rotational equation from (a) divided by $R$, $T_1 - T_2 = \dfrac{Ia}{R^2}$ (M1):
$$m_1g - m_2g - (T_1 - T_2) = (m_1 + m_2)a \quad \Rightarrow \quad (m_1 - m_2)g - \frac{Ia}{R^2} = (m_1 + m_2)a,$$
so $(m_1 - m_2)g = a\left(m_1 + m_2 + \dfrac{I}{R^2}\right)$ and the result follows (AG).

(c) First $\dfrac{I}{R^2} = \dfrac{0.0180}{0.120^2} = \dfrac{0.0180}{0.0144} = 1.25\,\mathrm{kg}$ (A1), so the effective inertia is $4.00 + 2.00 + 1.25 = 7.25\,\mathrm{kg}$. Hence
$$a = \frac{(4.00 - 2.00)(9.81)}{7.25} = \frac{19.62}{7.25} = 2.71\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \quad (\mathrm{A1}).$$
From the linear equations: $T_1 = m_1(g - a) = 4.00(9.81 - 2.7062) = 28.4\,\mathrm{N}$ (A1) and $T_2 = m_2(g + a) = 2.00(9.81 + 2.7062) = 25.0\,\mathrm{N}$ (A1).
Verification: $T_1 - T_2 = 28.415 - 25.032 = 3.383\,\mathrm{N}$, so the resultant torque is $3.383 \times 0.120 = 0.4059\,\mathrm{N\,m}$. Also $\alpha = \dfrac{a}{R} = \dfrac{2.7062}{0.120} = 22.55\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}$ and $I\alpha = 0.0180 \times 22.55 = 0.4059\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, which agrees (A1).

(d) With a massless pulley, $a_0 = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{19.62}{6.00} = 3.27\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (A1). Half of this is $1.635\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so (M1)
$$\frac{19.62}{6.00 + \frac{I}{R^2}} = 1.635 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 6.00 + \frac{I}{R^2} = \frac{19.62}{1.635} = 12.0,$$
giving the equivalent mass $\dfrac{I}{R^2} = 6.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ (A1) and hence
$$I = 6.00 \times 0.120^2 = 6.00 \times 0.0144 = 0.0864\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2} \quad (\mathrm{A1}).$$
This is $4.8$ times the original moment of inertia, which is why the acceleration falls by only a factor of two: doubling the effective inertia from $6.00$ to $12.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ is exactly what halving the acceleration requires.
questions.explanation:
The physics here is one idea wearing several costumes: the pulley has to be spun up, and spinning it up costs torque. That cost is why the two tensions differ, and the difference between the two tensions is the only thing in the problem that knows the moment of inertia exists.

The quantity $I/R^2$ deserves attention because it is the point where most candidates lose the thread. It has the units of kilograms and it sits in the formula added to two genuine masses, but it is not a mass: nothing is being lifted that weighs $I/R^2$ newtons. It is the rotational inertia of the pulley expressed in the translational units the rest of the problem is using, and the conversion factor is $1/R^2$ because the pulley's rim has to move at the same speed as the string. A candidate who understands this can predict the direction of the answer: a heavier pulley reduces the acceleration but never reverses it, and the limit of a very heavy pulley is $a \to 0$, not something else.

Part (d) is built to expose whether that understanding is there. The question asks for the moment of inertia that halves the acceleration, and the natural guess is that it doubles the moment of inertia. It does not: it takes the effective inertia from $6.00$ kg to $12.0$ kg, which means adding $6.00$ kg of equivalent mass, which is $4.8$ times the original pulley. The factor $4.8$ is not a round number and cannot be guessed, so the part discriminates cleanly.

This is adapted from the US AP Physics C: Mechanics treatment of the Atwood machine with a massive pulley. The AP version typically supplies the rotational equation and asks for the acceleration. Here the reasoning about why the tensions differ is asked for explicitly, the general formula is derived rather than given, and the final part inverts the relationship -- asking for the inertia that produces a stated acceleration, which is a different direction of travel from anything the source asks.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.1 Which oscillators feel an accelerating reference frame and which do not
questions.question:
A lift accelerates upwards at a constant $a = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Take
$g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Inside the lift are two oscillators.

* A simple pendulum of length $L = 0.80\ \mathrm{m}$.
* A mass–spring system: a mass $m = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ hanging from a spring of
spring constant $k = 200\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$.

(a) Show that, in the frame of the accelerating lift, the effective gravitational field
strength is $g + a$, and state its value. \tag{3}

(b) Find the period of the pendulum in the accelerating lift. \tag{4}

(c) Find the period of the mass–spring system in the accelerating lift, and explain why it has
the same value as when the lift is at rest. \tag{4}

(d) The acceleration of the lift is now unknown. The period of the pendulum is measured to be
$1.600\ \mathrm{s}$. Determine $a$. \tag{4}

(a)

Show that the effective gravitational field strength in the lift is $g + a$ and state its value.

[3]

(b)

Find the period of the pendulum in the accelerating lift.

[4]

(c)

Find the period of the mass–spring system in the accelerating lift, and explain why it matches the value at rest.

[4]

(d)

The pendulum's period is measured to be $1.600\ \mathrm{s}$. Determine the lift's acceleration $a$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) In the non-inertial frame of the lift there is a fictitious force $ma$ downwards on
every mass $m$ (M1), in addition to the weight $mg$ downwards. The total downward force is

$$F = mg + ma = m(g + a) \tag{A1}$$

so the effective gravitational field strength is $g_{\text{eff}} = g + a = 9.81 + 2.0
= 11.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (A1). Equivalently, an object released in the lift falls with
acceleration $g + a$ relative to the lift.

(b) For a simple pendulum the restoring force is the component of the effective weight along
the arc, so the standard result holds with $g$ replaced by $g + a$ (M1):

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g + a}} \tag{A1}$$

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.80}{11.81}} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.06774} = 2\pi(0.2603) = 1.64\ \mathrm{s}
\tag{A1}$$

For comparison, at rest the same pendulum has $T_{0} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.80}{9.81}} = 1.79\
\mathrm{s}$, so the acceleration shortens the period by about $9\%$ (A1). The amplitude does
not enter, as always for small oscillations.

(c) For a mass on a spring the restoring force is $-k$ times the extension, which has nothing
to do with gravity (M1). At equilibrium in the lift the spring is stretched by

$$x_{0} = \frac{m(g + a)}{k} = \frac{0.50 \times 11.81}{200} = 0.0295\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1}$$

against $x_{0} = \frac{0.50 \times 9.81}{200} = 0.0245\ \mathrm{m}$ at rest, so the
acceleration shifts the equilibrium position downwards by $5.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ and nothing else.
Displacing the mass by a further $y$ from that new equilibrium gives the net force

$$F = -k(x_{0} + y) + m(g + a) = -ky \tag{A1}$$

since $kx_{0} = m(g + a)$ by definition of the equilibrium position. This is SHM with
$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$, so

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.50}{200}} = 2\pi(0.0500) = 0.314\ \mathrm{s}
\tag{A1}$$

exactly as at rest. The acceleration has dropped out entirely, because it is a constant force
and a constant force can only move the centre of oscillation, not change the curvature of the
potential about that centre.

(d) Rearranging the result of (b),

$$g + a = \frac{4\pi^{2}L}{T^{2}} = \frac{4\pi^{2} \times 0.80}{1.600^{2}}
= \frac{31.58}{2.560} = 12.34\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \tag{M1}$$

$$a = 12.34 - 9.81 = 2.53\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \tag{A1}$$

Only the pendulum measurement is of any use here (A1): the period of the mass–spring system is
$0.314\ \mathrm{s}$ whatever the lift is doing, so it carries no information about $a$ at all.
A candidate who tries to extract $a$ from the spring period will find the algebra returns no
solution, which is the correct outcome (A1).
questions.explanation:
The result that a spring-mass oscillator ignores a uniform acceleration surprises people,
and the reason is short enough to be worth stating precisely: what sets the period of any
oscillator is the *curvature* of the potential at equilibrium, and a constant force tilts the
potential without curving it. Adding a constant downward force moves the equilibrium point and
leaves the second derivative exactly where it was, so $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ is
untouched.

The pendulum is different because gravity is not an added constant there — it *is* the
restoring force. The restoring torque comes from the component of weight along the arc, so
increasing the effective weight increases the restoring torque in direct proportion, and the
period shortens as $\frac{1}{\sqrt{g + a}}$. The same force that is irrelevant to the spring is
the whole mechanism for the pendulum.

This is why the item gives both oscillators and asks about both in the same lift. Any single
one of them could be answered by a memorised formula. Placed together, they force the question
"where does the restoring force come from?", and that question has a different answer for each.

Part (d) turns the distinction into something measurable. If you want to know how fast a lift
is accelerating, a pendulum is an accelerometer and a mass on a spring is not. The spring's
period carries no information, and the honest answer is not an approximate value of $a$ but the
statement that no value can be extracted. Candidates who have internalised the result in (c)
will say so immediately; candidates who have only memorised that "the period of a spring
does not depend on $g$" often try the substitution anyway and get stuck.

The numbers are chosen so that the effect is visible but not absurd: an acceleration of
$2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is a fifth of a gee, which shortens the pendulum period from
$1.79\ \mathrm{s}$ to $1.64\ \mathrm{s}$, about nine per cent. That is easily measurable with a
stopwatch over twenty oscillations, which is the practical reason the distinction matters.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.3 Friction on an incline depends on the normal reaction, so the two surfaces are not equivalent
questions.question:
A block of mass $m = 2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ is released from rest at the top of a slope of length
$s = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ inclined at $\theta = 30^\circ$ to the horizontal. It slides down the
slope and then continues on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction is
$\mu = 0.20$ on both surfaces. Take $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(a) Show that the acceleration of the block down the slope is $3.21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. \tag{3}

(b) Find the speed of the block when it reaches the bottom of the slope. \tag{4}

(c) Find the distance the block travels along the horizontal surface before coming to rest.
\tag{4}

(d) A student claims that the total work done against friction is $\mu mg(s + d)$, where $d$
is the distance found in (c). Explain why this is wrong, and determine the correct value of
the total work done against friction. \tag{4}

(a)

Show that the acceleration of the block down the slope is $3.21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

[3]

(b)

Find the speed of the block when it reaches the bottom of the slope.

[4]

(c)

Find the distance the block travels along the horizontal surface before coming to rest.

[4]

(d)

Explain why the total work done against friction is not $\mu mg(s + d)$, and determine its correct value.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Resolving perpendicular to the slope, the normal reaction is
$N = mg\cos\theta$ (M1). The friction is $f = \mu N = \mu mg\cos\theta$ (A1), so resolving
down the slope,

$$ma = mg\sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta) \tag{A1}$$

$$a = 9.81(\sin 30^\circ - 0.20\cos 30^\circ) = 9.81(0.500 - 0.173) = 9.81(0.327)
= 3.21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$$

Note that the mass cancels, as it must.

(b) With $u = 0$ and constant acceleration over $s = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ (M1),

$$v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as = 0 + 2(3.206)(4.0) = 25.65\ \mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-2}} \tag{A1}$$

$$v = 5.06\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \tag{A1}$$

Equivalently by energy: the loss of gravitational potential energy is
$mgh = mg s\sin\theta = 2.0 \times 9.81 \times 4.0 \times 0.5 = 39.2\ \mathrm{J}$ and the work
against friction on the slope is $\mu mg\cos\theta \times s = 13.6\ \mathrm{J}$, leaving
$25.6\ \mathrm{J}$ of kinetic energy, which gives the same speed (A1).

(c) On the horizontal surface the normal reaction is $N = mg$ (M1), so the retardation is

$$a' = \frac{\mu mg}{m} = \mu g = 0.20 \times 9.81 = 1.962\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \tag{A1}$$

and, with final speed zero,

$$d = \frac{v^{2}}{2a'} = \frac{25.65}{2 \times 1.962} = \frac{25.65}{3.924}
= 6.54\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1}$$

Alternatively, the remaining $25.6\ \mathrm{J}$ is dissipated over $d$ at
$\mu mg = 3.92\ \mathrm{N}$, giving the same result (A1).

(d) The expression $\mu mg(s + d)$ assumes the normal reaction is $mg$ over the whole path
(M1). It is not: on the slope the reaction is $mg\cos\theta$ (R1), so the friction on the
slope is smaller than $\mu mg$ by a factor of $\cos 30^\circ = 0.866$. The correct total is
the sum of the work on each surface (M1):

$$W = \mu mg\cos\theta \cdot s + \mu mg \cdot d
= (0.20)(2.0)(9.81)(0.866)(4.0) + (0.20)(2.0)(9.81)(6.54) \tag{A1}$$

$$= 13.6 + 25.6 = 39.2\ \mathrm{J}$$

which equals the loss of gravitational potential energy $mgh = 39.2\ \mathrm{J}$, as it must
(A1). The student's expression gives $3.924 \times (4.0 + 6.54) = 41.3\ \mathrm{J}$, which
exceeds the $39.2\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy available — a result that is impossible, and a useful
check to perform before accepting any answer of this kind. Working backwards from the
student's expression would give a total distance of $10.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and hence
$d = 6.0\ \mathrm{m}$, about $8\%$ short.
questions.explanation:
Friction is $\mu N$, and $N$ is not a property of the surfaces — it is a property of the
geometry. On the flat, $N = mg$. On a slope, $N = mg\cos\theta$. The coefficient is the same in
both places and it is the coefficient that the eye catches, which is exactly why the mistake is
common: everything in the stem encourages the candidate to treat $\mu$ as the whole story.

The consequence here is not small. The friction on the slope is $86.6\%$ of what it would be on
the flat, so using $\mu mg$ everywhere overestimates the energy dissipated on the way down by
about $1.7\ \mathrm{J}$ out of $39.2\ \mathrm{J}$. Over a total path of roughly ten metres that
is worth about half a metre of stopping distance, which is why the naive route gives
$d = 6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ instead of $6.54\ \mathrm{m}$.

What makes the error catchable is that it violates conservation of energy in a detectable way.
The student's total work against friction comes to $41.3\ \mathrm{J}$ while the block only ever
had $39.2\ \mathrm{J}$ of gravitational potential energy to spend. An answer that requires more
energy than the system possesses is not a slight misestimate; it is a signal that one term in
the sum has been computed with the wrong normal reaction. Checking a work calculation against
the energy budget should be a reflex, and part (d) is designed to make it one.

The item also illustrates a useful general habit about inclined planes: resolve perpendicular
first. The normal reaction is what friction, and anything else depending on contact, is
ultimately built from, and on a slope it is never $mg$.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme D: Fields
questions.subtopic: D.1 Total energy of a satellite in circular orbit, and why raising an orbit slows the satellite down
questions.question:
A satellite of mass $m = 800\ \mathrm{kg}$ is in a circular orbit of radius
$r = 7.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ about the Earth. Take
$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,kg^{-2}}$ and
$M = 5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$ for the mass of the Earth.

(a) Show that the kinetic energy of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is

$$E_{K} = \frac{GMm}{2r}. \tag{3}$$

(b) Hence show that the total energy of the satellite is

$$E = -\frac{GMm}{2r},$$

and calculate its value. \tag{5}

(c) Determine the energy that must be supplied to move the satellite into a circular orbit of
radius $2r$. \tag{3}

(d) Show that the satellite is moving more slowly in the larger orbit even though energy has
been supplied to it, and determine the ratio of the two speeds. \tag{4}

(a)

Show that the kinetic energy in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is $E_{K} = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.

[3]

(b)

Hence show that the total energy is $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and calculate its value.

[5]

(c)

Determine the energy that must be supplied to move the satellite into a circular orbit of radius $2r$.

[3]

(d)

Show that the satellite moves more slowly in the larger orbit, and determine the ratio of the two speeds.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) For a circular orbit the gravitational force supplies the centripetal force (M1):

$$\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v^{2} = \frac{GM}{r} \tag{A1}$$

Hence

$$E_{K} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{1}{2}m\frac{GM}{r} = \frac{GMm}{2r} \tag{AG}$$

(b) Taking gravitational potential energy as zero at infinity, the potential energy at radius
$r$ is $E_{P} = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ (M1). Adding the kinetic energy from (a) (M1),

$$E = E_{K} + E_{P} = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r} \tag{A1}$$

Numerically, $GM = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.97 \times 10^{24} = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\
\mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-2}}$, so (A1)

$$E = -\frac{3.98 \times 10^{14} \times 800}{2 \times 7.0 \times 10^{6}}
= -\frac{3.19 \times 10^{17}}{1.4 \times 10^{7}} = -2.28 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J} \tag{A1}$$

The total energy is negative, which is what "bound" means: the satellite does not have enough
energy to escape. Note also that $E = -E_{K}$, a relation that holds for every circular orbit
and is often the fastest way to check a result of this kind.

(c) At radius $2r$ the total energy is

$$E' = -\frac{GMm}{2(2r)} = -\frac{GMm}{4r} = \frac{E}{2} = -1.14 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}
\tag{M1}$$

so the energy that must be supplied is (A1)

$$\Delta E = E' - E = -\frac{GMm}{4r} + \frac{GMm}{2r} = \frac{GMm}{4r}
= 1.14 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J} \tag{A1}$$

Note what this is *not*. Using $mg\,\Delta h$ with $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and
$\Delta h = r = 7.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ gives
$800 \times 9.81 \times 7.0 \times 10^{6} = 5.49 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$, nearly five times
too large, because $g$ is not constant over a distance comparable with the radius of the Earth.

(d) From (a), $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ (M1), so

$$\frac{v_{2r}}{v_{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM/(2r)}{GM/r}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} = 0.707 \tag{A1}$$

The speed in the larger orbit is about $71\%$ of the speed in the smaller one, so the satellite
is unambiguously moving more slowly (A1). The kinetic energy correspondingly halves, from
$2.28 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$ to $1.14 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$, while the total energy
rises from $-2.28 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$ to $-1.14 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$. There is no
contradiction: the energy supplied has gone into gravitational potential energy, which
increases by $2.28 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$, while the kinetic energy falls by
$1.14 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1). Roughly, half the energy supplied raises the orbit and
the other half pays for the satellite's lost kinetic energy.
questions.explanation:
The expression $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ is one of those results that is easy to memorise and
easy to misuse, so the item makes the candidate build it in two steps: the kinetic energy from
the force balance, and then the sum with the potential energy. The building is quick, and it
buys something a memorised formula does not — the relation $E = -E_{K}$, which falls out of the
algebra and is the fastest available check on any circular-orbit calculation.

The interesting part is part (d), and it is genuinely counter-intuitive. Supplying energy to a
satellite makes it go slower. The resolution is that "lifting" and "speeding up" are not the
same thing, and the energy budget keeps separate accounts for them. Moving from $r$ to $2r$
increases the gravitational potential energy by $2.28 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$ and decreases
the kinetic energy by half that, so the net requirement is the difference,
$1.14 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$. A satellite in a higher orbit is higher up and slower, and
both of those are consequences of the same virial relation.

Part (c) contains the trap that is easiest to fall into and hardest to notice: reaching for
$mg\,\Delta h$. It is worth being explicit about why it fails so badly here. The formula
$mg\,\Delta h$ is the *uniform-field* approximation, valid when $\Delta h$ is small compared
with the radius of the Earth. Here $\Delta h = 7.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ is comparable
with the Earth's radius itself, so the field strength falls from about $8.1\
\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ at the lower orbit to about $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ at the upper one, and
using the surface value throughout gives an answer nearly five times too big. The general
lesson: before using a constant-$g$ formula, check that the distance involved is small compared
with the scale over which $g$ changes.

The item also quietly makes the point that a bound orbit has negative total energy, and that
"more bound" means more negative. The satellite in the lower orbit has *less* total energy
($-2.28 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$) than the one in the higher orbit ($-1.14 \times 10^{10}\
\mathrm{J}$), which is why energy has to be supplied to go up, even though the satellite ends
up with less kinetic energy than it started with.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.question:
The diagram shows two cells connected in parallel between the junctions A and B, together with a resistor R of resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ connected between the same two junctions. Cell 1 has emf $\varepsilon_{1}=12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $r_{1}=0.40\ \Omega$; cell 2 has emf $\varepsilon_{2}=9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $r_{2}=0.60\ \Omega$. The connecting wires have negligible resistance.

(a)

By applying $\varepsilon=I(R+r)$ to each source branch, and by requiring that the current arriving at junction A equals the current leaving it, show that the potential difference between A and B is $9.64\ \mathrm{V}$.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the current in each of the two source branches, stating the direction of each current, and calculate the current in R.

[4]

(c)

Show that the total power delivered by cell 1 equals the sum of the power dissipated in the two internal resistances, the power dissipated in R, and the power absorbed by cell 2.

[4]

(d)

Determine the value of $\varepsilon_{2}$ for which no current flows in branch 2, leaving $\varepsilon_{1}$, $r_{1}$ and $R$ unchanged.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Let $V$ be the potential difference between A and B. In branch 1 the current is $I_{1}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{1}-V}{r_{1}}$ and in branch 2 it is $I_{2}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{2}-V}{r_{2}}$, while the current in R is $I=\dfrac{V}{R}$. (M1)

Current is conserved at junction A, so $I_{1}+I_{2}=I$: (M1)

$$\frac{12.0-V}{0.40}+\frac{9.0-V}{0.60}=\frac{V}{2.0}$$

Multiplying throughout by $1.2$: $3(12.0-V)+2(9.0-V)=0.6V$. (M1)

So $36.0-3V+18.0-2V=0.6V$, giving $54.0=5.6V$ and $V=9.64\ \mathrm{V}$. (AG)

(b) $I_{1}=\dfrac{12.0-9.643}{0.40}=5.89\ \mathrm{A}$ (M1)(A1), flowing from the positive terminal of cell 1 through junction A and out into the rest of the circuit.

$I_{2}=\dfrac{9.0-9.643}{0.60}=-1.07\ \mathrm{A}$ (M1), so a current of $1.07\ \mathrm{A}$ flows into the positive terminal of cell 2: cell 1 is charging cell 2. (A1)

The current in R is $I=\dfrac{9.643}{2.0}=4.82\ \mathrm{A}$. (A1)

Check: $5.893-1.071=4.821\ \mathrm{A}$, consistent with current conservation.

(c) Power delivered by cell 1: $\varepsilon_{1}I_{1}=12.0\times 5.893=70.7\ \mathrm{W}$. (M1)

Power dissipated in the two internal resistances: $I_{1}^{2}r_{1}=5.893^{2}\times 0.40=13.9\ \mathrm{W}$ and $I_{2}^{2}r_{2}=1.071^{2}\times 0.60=0.689\ \mathrm{W}$. (M1)

Power dissipated in R: $\dfrac{V^{2}}{R}=\dfrac{9.643^{2}}{2.0}=46.5\ \mathrm{W}$. (M1)

Power absorbed by cell 2, which is being charged: $\varepsilon_{2}I_{2}=9.0\times 1.071=9.64\ \mathrm{W}$.

Total $=13.89+0.689+46.49+9.64=70.7\ \mathrm{W}$, which equals the power delivered by cell 1. (A1)

(d) No current in branch 2 requires $V=\varepsilon_{2}$, since branch 2 then has no potential difference across its internal resistance. (M1)

With $I_{2}=0$ the current in branch 1 equals the current in R: $\dfrac{12.0-V}{0.40}=\dfrac{V}{2.0}$, so $2(12.0-V)=0.40V$ and $24.0=2.4V$. (M1)

Hence $V=10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $\varepsilon_{2}=10.0\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The circuit looks symmetrical and is not. Two cells in parallel with different emfs cannot both deliver current: the potential difference settles between the two emfs, so the stronger cell drives current backwards through the weaker one. Students who assume both cells supply current will set up two positive branch currents, reach a value of $V$ above $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$, and produce an inconsistent current balance without noticing. The sign of $I_{2}$ is the whole point of the question, and part (b) asks for the direction explicitly to make sure it is confronted.

The power audit in part (c) is the strongest check available, and it is worth doing whenever a circuit contains more than one source. Cell 2 absorbs energy at the rate $\varepsilon_{2}I_{2}$ in addition to dissipating $I_{2}^{2}r_{2}$ in its own internal resistance. The two terms are different: the first is energy converted into chemical energy in the cell being charged, the second is energy lost as heat inside it. Omitting the first term is the standard error and it leaves about 14% of the power unaccounted for, which is why the question asks for the audit rather than for a single value.

Part (d) inverts the reasoning. Rather than solving for $V$ given the emfs, it asks what emf would make a branch carry no current, and the answer is that the cell's emf must equal the potential difference across it — the condition for a cell neither charging nor discharging. It is a short part but it tests whether the mechanism behind the terminal potential difference has been understood rather than memorised.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme D: Fields
questions.question:
Two long parallel rails, separated by a distance $L=0.60\ \mathrm{m}$, lie in a horizontal plane and are frictionless. A straight conducting rod of mass $m=0.12\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests across the rails and can slide along them. The rails and the rod have negligible resistance, and a resistor of resistance $R=0.80\ \Omega$ connects the rails at one end. Over the whole region between the rails there is a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B=0.45\ \mathrm{T}$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the rails. A light inextensible string attached to the rod passes over a frictionless pulley and supports a hanging mass $m_{2}=0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$. The system is released from rest.

(a)

Show that the rod reaches a terminal speed and derive an expression for that speed in terms of $m_{2}$, $g$, $R$, $B$ and $L$. Calculate its value.

[6]

(b)

Show that, at the terminal speed, the rate at which the hanging mass loses gravitational potential energy equals the rate at which energy is dissipated in the resistor.

[3]

(c)

The flux density is doubled to $0.90\ \mathrm{T}$ with everything else unchanged. Determine the new terminal speed and explain why the change is larger than a factor of two.

[3]

(d)

Instead the rod is replaced by a longer rod of the same mass that spans rails a distance $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ apart, with the field restored to $0.45\ \mathrm{T}$. Determine the new terminal speed and explain why it is numerically the same as your answer to part (c).

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) As the rod accelerates, the emf induced across it is $\varepsilon=BvL$ and the current around the circuit is $I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{BvL}{R}$. The magnetic force opposing the motion is $F=BIL=\dfrac{B^{2}L^{2}v}{R}$. (M1)(M1)

For the rod and hanging mass moving together, the resultant driving force is $m_{2}g-F$, so $m_{2}g-\dfrac{B^{2}L^{2}v}{R}=(m+m_{2})a$. (M1)

As $v$ increases the opposing force grows, so $a$ falls; when $m_{2}g=\dfrac{B^{2}L^{2}v}{R}$ the acceleration is zero and the speed stops changing. (A1)

Hence $v=\dfrac{m_{2}gR}{B^{2}L^{2}}$. (A1)

Numerically $v=\dfrac{0.050\times 9.81\times 0.80}{(0.45)^{2}(0.60)^{2}}=\dfrac{0.3924}{0.0729}=5.38\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1)

(b) At terminal speed the current is $I=\dfrac{BvL}{R}=\dfrac{0.45\times 5.383\times 0.60}{0.80}=1.82\ \mathrm{A}$. (M1)

Power dissipated in the resistor: $I^{2}R=(1.8167)^{2}\times 0.80=2.64\ \mathrm{W}$. (A1)

Rate of loss of gravitational potential energy of the hanging mass: $m_{2}gv=0.050\times 9.81\times 5.383=2.64\ \mathrm{W}$, equal to the electrical power. (A1) This is the content of Lenz's law: the induced current dissipates energy at exactly the rate at which mechanical energy is supplied, so no energy is created in the circuit.

(c) Since $v\propto\dfrac{1}{B^{2}}$, doubling $B$ divides the terminal speed by four: $v=\dfrac{0.3924}{(0.90)^{2}(0.60)^{2}}=\dfrac{0.3924}{0.2916}=1.35\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (M1)(A1)

The effect is more than a factor of two because the field enters twice. Doubling $B$ doubles the induced emf at a given speed, which on its own would double the current; but that doubled current also experiences twice the magnetic force per ampere. The two doublings compound, so the same retarding force is produced at one quarter of the speed. (A1)

(d) Since $v\propto\dfrac{1}{L^{2}}$ as well, doubling $L$ again divides the speed by four: $v=\dfrac{0.3924}{(0.45)^{2}(1.20)^{2}}=\dfrac{0.3924}{0.2916}=1.35\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (M1)(A1)

The two answers agree because $B$ and $L$ appear in the terminal-speed expression only through the product $BL$, which is the quantity that sets both the emf at a given speed and the force at a given current. Doubling either one therefore produces exactly the same change, and the mass of the rod does not enter the expression at all, since at terminal speed the rod's own acceleration is zero. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The rod does not accelerate indefinitely, and the reason is worth stating precisely: the magnetic force is not constant but proportional to the speed. At rest there is no current and no magnetic force, so the driving weight accelerates the system; as the speed rises the induced emf rises, the current rises, and so does the retarding force. Equilibrium is reached when the retarding force equals the driving force, and thereafter the speed is constant even though the hanging mass continues to descend.

The important structural point is that the terminal condition is a force balance, not a statement that the acceleration is zero in some vague sense, and it is reached without solving the differential equation for $v(t)$. This is the same reasoning used for a falling object with air resistance, and recognising the pattern is half the work.

The two final parts are deliberately constructed to produce the same numerical answer by different routes. The expression is $v=m_{2}gR/(B^{2}L^{2})$, so both doubling $B$ and doubling $L$ divide the speed by four, because both quantities enter only through the product $BL$. That product appears once in the emf and once in the force, which is why the square appears. A student who works out that $B$ enters twice but treats $L$ as entering once — for instance by assuming the magnetic force is $BIL$ with $I$ independent of $L$ — will get part (d) wrong and, more importantly, will have missed the structure of the problem.

The mass of the rod never appears in the final answer, which surprises students who expect it to matter. It affects how quickly the terminal speed is reached, not what that speed is, and part (d) makes this concrete by doubling the length while holding the mass fixed.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.2 Hooke's law and A.3 the force constant from a gradient
questions.question:
A student hangs a series of masses on a vertical spring and records the extension of the spring for each mass. The readings are plotted in the figure, in which the extension $x$ is in centimetres and the hanging mass $m$ is in grams. The straight line shown is the line of best fit, drawn through the origin because the spring was set so that its extension was zero when no mass was hung. One reading, at $m = 250$ g, is labelled X. The spring has negligible mass and the masses hang in equilibrium. Answer all parts with reference to the data in the figure, and quote numerical answers to three significant figures. Take $g = 9.81$ N kg$^{-1}$.

(a)

Determine the gradient of the line of best fit, giving the unit of your answer.

[2]

(b)

Evaluate whether reading X should be included when the line of best fit is drawn, supporting your answer with a numerical comparison against the other readings.

[3]

(c)

Hence determine the force constant of the spring, in N m$^{-1}$, using the gradient of the line of best fit.

[3]

(d)

Suggest one source of uncertainty in the value of the gradient and explain how it would affect the value you obtained for the force constant.

[3]

(e)

The experiment is repeated with a second identical spring joined in series with the first, so that the two springs hang end to end and the masses hang from the lower spring. Suggest how the gradient of the graph and the force constant you calculated in part (c) would change, and justify your answer.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The line passes through the origin and through the reading at $m = 300$ g, where the line gives $x = 12.15$ cm. (M1) The gradient is therefore $12.15/300 = 0.0405$ cm g$^{-1}$. (A1)

(b) The line predicts $x = 0.0405(250) = 10.1$ cm at $m = 250$ g, but the recorded reading is 11.4 cm, so X lies 1.3 cm above the line. (M1) The other five readings lie within about 0.05 cm of the line, which is the scale of the random scatter, so the deviation of X is roughly twenty-five times larger than the scatter of the rest of the data. (A1) A single reading that far off the pattern is an anomalous reading, most likely a misread scale or a mass recorded wrongly, and it should be excluded from the line of best fit and investigated. (A1)

(c) Converting the gradient into SI units, $0.0405$ cm g$^{-1} = 0.0405 \times 10^{-2}$ m per $10^{-3}$ kg $= 0.405$ m kg$^{-1}$. (M1) In equilibrium $mg = kx$, so $x/m = g/k$ and hence $k = g/(x/m)$. (M1) Therefore $k = 9.81/0.405 = 24.2$ N m$^{-1}$. (A1)

(d) The gradient depends on how accurately the extension was read against the scale, and the smallest scale division limits how precisely each point can be placed. (A1) Reading each extension too large by a fixed amount, for example by taking the scale from the wrong mark, makes the gradient too large. (M1) Since $k = g/(x/m)$, an over-large gradient gives a force constant that is too small, so the uncertainty in $k$ is in the opposite direction to the error in the gradient. (A1)

(e) Each spring now supports the same force $mg$, so each extends by the same amount as the single spring did on its own. (M1) The total extension is therefore twice the extension of one spring for the same hanging mass, so the gradient doubles to 0.0810 cm g$^{-1}$. (A1)(A1) Since $k = g/(x/m)$ and the extension per unit mass has doubled, the force constant of the combination is $24.2/2 = 12.1$ N m$^{-1}$, which is the expected result for two identical springs in series. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The figure supplies the line of best fit already drawn, which moves the demand of this question away from plotting and onto interpretation. The line passes through the origin, because the spring was set to zero extension with no mass, and it rises to about 12.15 cm at 300 g, giving a gradient of 0.0405 cm per gram.

The interesting feature of the data is the reading at 250 g. The line predicts 10.1 cm there, and the recorded value is 11.4 cm, so the point sits 1.3 cm above the line while every other reading sits within about 0.05 cm of it. That is not scatter; it is a different kind of number. The right response is to exclude it, draw the line through the remaining five readings, and look for the cause. A candidate who keeps it will draw a steeper line and obtain a force constant that is too small.

Part (c) contains the trap that the item is really built around. The gradient is 0.0405 centimetres per gram, and a spring constant is measured in newtons per metre. Those units are three powers of ten apart in the length and three in the mass, and a candidate who divides $g$ by 0.0405 without converting gets 242 N m$^{-1}$, which is exactly ten times too large. The correct conversion gives 0.405 m kg$^{-1}$ and a force constant of 24.2 N m$^{-1}$.

Part (d) asks about uncertainty rather than asking for a calculation, and the important thing is the direction. If each extension is read slightly too large, the gradient comes out too large, and because the force constant is $g$ divided by the gradient, the force constant comes out too small. Getting the inverse relationship right is the mark that separates a candidate who understands the algebra from one who has only learned to substitute.

Part (e) changes the apparatus and leaves the data behind. Two identical springs in series each carry the full hanging weight, so each extends by the same amount the single spring did. The total extension doubles, the gradient doubles, and the force constant halves to 12.1 N m$^{-1}$. A candidate who tries to reuse the numbers from part (c) without thinking about the new arrangement will not find this.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme D: Fields
questions.question:
A satellite of mass $m$ is to be moved from a circular low Earth orbit of radius $r_{1}=6.87\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ to a circular geostationary orbit of radius $r_{2}=4.23\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$.

The manoeuvre is carried out in two burns. The first burn puts the satellite onto an elliptical transfer orbit whose perigee is $r_{1}$ and whose apogee is $r_{2}$. The second burn, at apogee, circularises the orbit.

The total energy of a satellite of mass $m$ in an elliptical orbit of semi-major axis $a$ is $E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$, where $M$ is the mass of Earth.

Data: $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,kg^{-2}}$, $M=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

(a)

Show that the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, and calculate the orbital speeds in the low orbit and in the geostationary orbit.

[3]

(b)

Show that the semi-major axis of the transfer orbit is $a=2.46\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$ and hence, using the expression for $E$ given above, show that the speed of the satellite at a distance $r$ from the centre of Earth on the transfer orbit satisfies $v^{2}=GM\left(\dfrac{2}{r}-\dfrac{1}{a}\right)$.

[4]

(c)

Calculate the speed of the satellite at perigee and at apogee of the transfer orbit. Hence determine the change in speed required at each burn and the total change in speed.

[4]

(d)

Determine the time of flight from perigee to apogee along the transfer orbit. Hence calculate the angle through which a satellite already in the geostationary orbit moves during that time, and state what this implies for the moment at which the first burn must be made.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) For a circular orbit the gravitational force provides the centripetal force:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^{2}}=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}.$$ (M1)

$GM=6.67\times10^{-11}\times5.97\times10^{24}=3.98\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-2}}$.

Low orbit: $v_{1}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3.98\times10^{14}}{6.87\times10^{6}}}=\sqrt{5.80\times10^{7}}=7.61\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (A1)

Geostationary: $v_{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3.98\times10^{14}}{4.23\times10^{7}}}=\sqrt{9.41\times10^{6}}=3.07\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (A1)

(b) $a=\dfrac{r_{1}+r_{2}}{2}=\dfrac{6.87\times10^{6}+4.23\times10^{7}}{2}=2.46\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$ (A1)

On the ellipse, $E=\tfrac12mv^{2}-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ (M1) (kinetic + gravitational potential energy)

Equating to the given total energy:

$$\tfrac12mv^{2}-\frac{GMm}{r}=-\frac{GMm}{2a}\ \Rightarrow\ \tfrac12v^{2}=\frac{GM}{r}-\frac{GM}{2a}$$ (M1)

$$\Rightarrow\ v^{2}=GM\left(\frac{2}{r}-\frac{1}{a}\right).\ \ \textbf{(A1)}$$ *(AG)*

(c) At perigee, $r=r_{1}=6.87\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$:

$$v_{\text{per}}^{2}=3.98\times10^{14}\left(\frac{2}{6.87\times10^{6}}-\frac{1}{2.4585\times10^{7}}\right)=3.98\times10^{14}\left(2.911\times10^{-7}-4.068\times10^{-8}\right)=9.97\times10^{7}$$

$v_{\text{per}}=9.99\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (A1)

$$\Delta v_{1}=9.99-7.61=2.37\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ \ (2.37\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}})$$ (A1)

At apogee, $r=r_{2}=4.23\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$:

$$v_{\text{apo}}^{2}=3.98\times10^{14}\left(\frac{2}{4.23\times10^{7}}-\frac{1}{2.4585\times10^{7}}\right)=3.98\times10^{14}\left(4.728\times10^{-8}-4.068\times10^{-8}\right)=2.63\times10^{6}$$

$v_{\text{apo}}=1.62\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (A1)

$$\Delta v_{2}=3.07-1.62=1.45\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad \Delta v_{\text{total}}=2.37+1.45=3.82\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

(d) Period of the transfer ellipse: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{a^{3}}{GM}}$

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(2.4585\times10^{7})^{3}}{3.98\times10^{14}}}=2\pi\sqrt{3.73\times10^{7}}=3.84\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s}$$ (M1)

Time of flight $=\tfrac12T=1.92\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s}=5.33\,\mathrm{h}$ (A1)

Period of the geostationary orbit: $T_{\text{geo}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(4.23\times10^{7})^{3}}{3.98\times10^{14}}}=8.66\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s}\;(=24.1\,\mathrm{h})$

$$\theta=360^{\circ}\times\frac{1.92\times10^{4}}{8.66\times10^{4}}=79.8^{\circ}\approx80^{\circ}$$ (A1)

The spacecraft travels through $180^{\circ}$ around Earth, so the target must be $180^{\circ}-80^{\circ}\approx100^{\circ}$ ahead of the launch position at the instant of the first burn, so that both arrive at the same point at the same time. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Two ideas have to be held at once, and both are counter-intuitive.

First, the circular-orbit formula $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ does not give the speed on the transfer orbit. On an ellipse the total energy is fixed by the semi-major axis alone, so the speed follows from $\tfrac12v^{2}-\frac{GM}{r}=-\frac{GM}{2a}$: the satellite's speed at any point is set by where it is *and* by the size of the whole orbit. Using $\sqrt{GM/r_{1}}$ at perigee is the single most common error.

Second, the 'paradox'. The satellite finishes in an orbit whose speed (3.07 km s⁻¹) is far lower than where it started (7.61 km s⁻¹), so it is natural to expect the second burn to slow it down. It does not: arriving at apogee it is crawling at only 1.62 km s⁻¹, well below the 3.07 km s⁻¹ needed to stay there, so the second burn is also a speed-up. Both burns are prograde, and the total $\Delta v$ of 3.82 km s⁻¹ is what the mission actually costs in fuel.

Part (d) supplies the operational point: a transfer is not available on demand. The launch window recurs each time the geometry repeats, which is why interplanetary missions have narrow windows rather than daily departures.

Classic wrong turns: using $r_{1}$ or $r_{2}$ in place of $a$ in the energy expression; treating the flight time as half the period of either circular orbit; and computing the lead angle as 80° instead of 100°.

A less obvious wrong turn sits in part (d): candidates sometimes estimate the transfer period by averaging the periods of the two circular orbits, taking the ellipse to lie 'between' them. Kepler's third law is not linear in the radius — the period scales as $a^{3/2}$ — so the mean of the two periods is not the period of the ellipse. The semi-major axis of the transfer orbit is the mean of the two radii, but its period must be computed from that axis through the $3/2$ power, not averaged from the endpoint orbits.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.5 Systematic error from meter resistance, and why two wrong readings bracket the truth
questions.question:
A student determines an unknown resistance $X$ using a voltmeter of resistance
$R_{V} = 4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ and an ammeter of resistance $R_{A} = 2.0\ \Omega$, in the two
circuits described below.

Circuit 1. The voltmeter is connected directly across $X$. The ammeter is outside the
voltmeter, so it measures the current through $X$ and the current through the voltmeter
combined. The ratio of the voltmeter reading to the ammeter reading is $R_{1} = 97.6\ \Omega$.

Circuit 2. The ammeter is in series with $X$ and the voltmeter is connected across the
combination. The ratio of the voltmeter reading to the ammeter reading is
$R_{2} = 102\ \Omega$.

(a) Show that in circuit 1 the ratio of the readings is

$$R_{1} = \frac{X R_{V}}{X + R_{V}}. \tag{3}$$

(b) Show that in circuit 2 the ratio of the readings is

$$R_{2} = X + R_{A}. \tag{3}$$

(c) Hence determine the true value of $X$, and state the systematic error, in ohms, of each
circuit. \tag{4}

(d) Determine the value of $X$ for which the two circuits have systematic errors of equal
magnitude. \tag{4}

(a)

Show that in circuit 1 the ratio of the readings is $R_{1} = \dfrac{X R_{V}}{X + R_{V}}$.

[3]

(b)

Show that in circuit 2 the ratio of the readings is $R_{2} = X + R_{A}$.

[3]

(c)

Hence determine the true value of $X$, and state the systematic error, in ohms, of each circuit.

[4]

(d)

Determine the value of $X$ for which the two circuits have systematic errors of equal magnitude.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) In circuit 1 the voltmeter and $X$ are in parallel, so the voltage $V$ across them is
the same and the currents add (M1). The ammeter reads

$$I = I_{X} + I_{V} = \frac{V}{X} + \frac{V}{R_{V}} = V\left(\frac{1}{X} + \frac{1}{R_{V}}\right)
\tag{A1}$$

so the ratio of the readings is

$$R_{1} = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{X} + \dfrac{1}{R_{V}}} = \frac{X R_{V}}{X + R_{V}}
\tag{AG}$$

which is the parallel combination of $X$ and $R_{V}$. It is therefore always less than $X$.

(b) In circuit 2 the ammeter is in series with $X$, so it reads the true current $I$ through
$X$ (M1), while the voltmeter is across both and reads

$$V = I X + I R_{A} = I(X + R_{A}) \tag{A1}$$

so $R_{2} = \dfrac{V}{I} = X + R_{A}$ (AG). This reading is always greater than $X$, because
it includes the resistance of the ammeter itself.

(c) From (b), $X = R_{2} - R_{A} = 102 - 2.0 = 100\ \Omega$ (M1)(A1). Substituting back into
(a) as a check,

$$R_{1} = \frac{100 \times 4000}{100 + 4000} = \frac{400000}{4100} = 97.56\ \Omega \tag{A1}$$

which agrees with the reading of $97.6\ \Omega$ to the precision quoted. The systematic
errors are therefore

$$\text{circuit 1: } 97.56 - 100 = -2.44\ \Omega \qquad
\text{circuit 2: } 102 - 100 = +2.00\ \Omega \tag{A1}$$

so the two readings bracket the true value, the first low and the second high.

(d) The magnitude of the error in circuit 1 is

$$X - \frac{X R_{V}}{X + R_{V}} = \frac{X(X + R_{V}) - X R_{V}}{X + R_{V}} = \frac{X^{2}}{X + R_{V}}
\tag{M1}$$

and the magnitude of the error in circuit 2 is $R_{A}$ (A1). Setting them equal,

$$\frac{X^{2}}{X + R_{V}} = R_{A} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X^{2} - R_{A}X - R_{A}R_{V} = 0
\tag{M1}$$

$$X = \frac{R_{A} + \sqrt{R_{A}^{2} + 4R_{A}R_{V}}}{2}
= \frac{2.0 + \sqrt{4.0 + 4(2.0)(4000)}}{2} = \frac{2.0 + 178.9}{2} = 90.4\ \Omega \tag{A1}$$

The negative root is rejected as unphysical. Below about $90\ \Omega$ circuit 1 is the more
accurate of the two; above it, circuit 2 is. Note that the crossover is not where the two
readings are equal — it is where their *errors* are, and the two conditions are different.
questions.explanation:
Both circuits are wrong, and that is the point. A voltmeter with finite resistance
necessarily draws some current, and an ammeter with non-zero resistance necessarily drops some
voltage, so the ratio $V/I$ is never quite the resistance of the device under test. The
question is only whether the error is large enough to matter and whether it can be removed.

The two circuits fail in opposite directions, which is what makes the pair useful. Circuit 1
measures a parallel combination and therefore reads low; circuit 2 includes the ammeter in
series and therefore reads high. A candidate who takes one reading and stops has no way of
knowing which way the error went, but a candidate who takes both has bracketed the true value
and can locate it exactly, because circuit 2's error does not depend on $X$ at all — it is
just the ammeter's resistance, given in the stem.

Part (d) is where the item stops being a correction exercise and becomes a design question.
The error in circuit 1 grows with $X$ (roughly as $\frac{X^{2}}{R_{V}}$ while $X$ is small
compared with $R_{V}$), and the error in circuit 2 is the constant $R_{A}$. So there is a
crossing point: for small resistances the voltmeter's shunting effect is negligible and
circuit 1 wins, and for large resistances the ammeter's $2\ \Omega$ is negligible and circuit
2 wins. Working out where the crossing is — about $90\ \Omega$ here — is the practical content
of choosing a circuit.

The mistake the item is really fishing for appears at the end of the markscheme. Candidates
naturally equate the two *readings*, because that is what "find where they agree" usually
means. That is the wrong condition: what has to be equal is the size of the *errors*, and
since one reading is below $X$ and the other above, equality of readings cannot happen at all
for a value of $X$ that both circuits can measure. Keeping the two conditions apart is a
discipline worth more than the algebra.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.5 An echo from a moving reflector is Doppler shifted twice, not once
questions.question:
A bat flies towards a wall emitting ultrasound of frequency $f = 40.0\ \mathrm{kHz}$. The wall
moves towards the bat at speed $u = 12.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed of sound in air is
$c = 340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The situation is shown in the diagram.

A student argues that, since the wall is approaching the bat, the echo is Doppler shifted once
and its frequency is $f' = f\dfrac{c + u}{c}$.

(a) Show that the frequency received by the wall is

$$f_{1} = f\frac{c + u}{c},$$

and calculate $f_{1}$. \tag{4}

(b) Hence show that the frequency received back at the bat is

$$f_{2} = f\frac{c + u}{c - u},$$

and calculate $f_{2}$. \tag{5}

(c) Calculate the beat frequency detected by the bat. \tag{2}

(d) Explain why the student's single application of the Doppler formula underestimates the
shift. \tag{3}

(a)

Show that the frequency received by the wall is $f_{1} = f\dfrac{c + u}{c}$ and calculate it.

[4]

(b)

Hence show that the frequency received back at the bat is $f_{2} = f\dfrac{c + u}{c - u}$ and calculate it.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the beat frequency detected by the bat.

[2]

(d)

Explain why a single application of the Doppler formula underestimates the shift.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The source (the bat) is stationary relative to the air, so the wavelength in the air is
$\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$ (M1). The wall moves towards the source, so it meets wavefronts at the
relative speed $c + u$ (M1) and receives

$$f_{1} = \frac{c + u}{\lambda} = \frac{c + u}{c/f} = f\frac{c + u}{c} \tag{A1}$$

$$f_{1} = 40.0 \times \frac{340 + 12.0}{340} = 40.0 \times \frac{352}{340}
= 41.4\ \mathrm{kHz} \tag{A1}$$

(b) The wall now acts as a source of frequency $f_{1}$ — the frequency at which it receives
and re-radiates — and it moves towards the bat, so the wavefronts are compressed (M1). The
wavelength of the reflected sound in the air ahead of the wall is

$$\lambda' = \frac{c - u}{f_{1}} \tag{M1}$$

because the wall advances by $u$ during each period. The bat, stationary in the air, receives

$$f_{2} = \frac{c}{\lambda'} = \frac{c f_{1}}{c - u} = f\frac{c + u}{c - u} \tag{A1}$$

$$f_{2} = 40.0 \times \frac{352}{328} = 40.0 \times 1.0732 = 42.9\ \mathrm{kHz} \tag{A1}$$

Equivalently, $f_{2} = f_{1} \times \frac{340}{328} = 41.41 \times 1.0366 = 42.9\
\mathrm{kHz}$ (A1).

(c) The bat hears both the emitted $40.0\ \mathrm{kHz}$ and the returned $42.9\
\mathrm{kHz}$ simultaneously, so the beat frequency is

$$f_{\text{beat}} = f_{2} - f = 42.93 - 40.0 = 2.93\ \mathrm{kHz} \tag{A1}$$

which is well within a bat's audible range (A1).

(d) The student's $f' = f\frac{c+u}{c}$ is the frequency at the *wall*, not the frequency back
at the bat (A1). The shift happens twice because the wall changes role between the two legs of
the journey: it is a moving observer on the way out and a moving source on the way back (R1).
Each stage multiplies the frequency by a factor greater than one, so the two-stage result
exceeds the one-stage result by the factor $\frac{c}{c-u} = 1.037$, about $3.7\%$ (A1). The
student's value $41.4\ \mathrm{kHz}$ against the true $42.9\ \mathrm{kHz}$ understates the beat
frequency by more than half: $1.41\ \mathrm{kHz}$ instead of $2.93\ \mathrm{kHz}$.
questions.explanation:
The Doppler effect is usually taught as two separate formulae — one for a moving source
and one for a moving observer — and the usual drill is to decide which one applies and use it.
That drill has no answer here, because the reflector is both, one after the other.

On the outward leg the bat is stationary in the air and the wall moves, so the wall is a moving
observer: it runs into wavefronts at $c + u$ and receives a frequency higher by the factor
$\frac{c+u}{c}$. On the return leg the wall is the source of the reflected sound, and because
it advances during each period the wavefronts it emits are squeezed into a wavelength
$\frac{c-u}{f_{1}}$; the bat, stationary, receives a frequency higher again by the factor
$\frac{c}{c-u}$. The two factors multiply.

The product is not quite the same as applying one of them twice. Because the two formulae have
different denominators — $c$ for the moving observer and $c - u$ for the moving source — the
exact result is $\frac{c+u}{c-u}$, whereas doubling the single-stage shift would give
$1 + \frac{2u}{c}$. At $u = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $c = 340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ the two
differ by about $3.7\%$, which is small but not negligible, and it is the sort of discrepancy
that shows up when a candidate tries to check an exact expression against a rule of thumb.

The physical reason the shift is applied twice is worth separating from the algebra: an echo is
not a reflection in the mirror sense. The wall does not simply bounce the wave back with the
frequency it arrived with; it re-radiates, and while it re-radiates it is moving. This is why
Doppler ultrasound and radar speed guns both work on the two-stage formula, and why the shift
they measure is roughly double what a single application would predict.

Part (c) is a small but deliberate addition. A bat listening to its own echo is listening to two
frequencies at once, and what it actually detects is the beat between them. Stating the beat
frequency rather than the returned frequency grounds the calculation in what the animal hears.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.5 Current and circuits: e.m.f., internal resistance and power
questions.question:
The figure shows a cell of electromotive force $E$ and internal resistance $r$ connected in series with two resistors, $R_1$ and $R_2$, and with a voltmeter connected across $R_2$. The cell has $E = 6.0$ V and $r = 0.50$ $\Omega$, and the resistors have $R_1 = 4.0$ $\Omega$ and $R_2 = 6.0$ $\Omega$ as marked on the diagram. The ammeter and the connecting wires have negligible resistance. In parts (a) to (d) the voltmeter may be treated as ideal, and in part (c) it may not. Give all numerical answers to three significant figures.

(a)

Calculate the current in the circuit, treating the voltmeter as ideal.

[2]

(b)

Determine the reading on the voltmeter, treating the voltmeter as ideal.

[2]

(c)

The voltmeter is now known to have a resistance of 1.0 k$\Omega$ rather than being ideal. State, and explain, how the reading it gives compares with the reading you found in part (b).

[3]

(d)

Calculate the efficiency of the circuit, defined as the fraction of the total power supplied by the cell that is dissipated in $R_1$ and $R_2$.

[3]

(e)

$R_2$ is now replaced by a variable resistor of resistance $R$. Determine the value of $R$ for which the power dissipated in it is a maximum, and determine that maximum power. Show your reasoning.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The cell drives current through $R_1$, $R_2$ and its own internal resistance in series, so the total resistance is $4.0 + 6.0 + 0.50 = 10.5$ $\Omega$. (M1) Applying $I = E/R_{total}$ gives $I = 6.0/10.5 = 0.571$ A. (A1)

(b) The voltmeter is connected across $R_2$ only, so it reads the potential difference across that resistor alone. (M1) $V = IR_2 = 0.5714 \times 6.0 = 3.43$ V. (A1)

(c) A real voltmeter of resistance 1.0 k$\Omega$ is in parallel with $R_2$, so the resistance of that branch is slightly less than 6.0 $\Omega$, not more. (M1) The parallel combination is $\frac{(6.0)(1000)}{1006} = 5.964$ $\Omega$, so the total resistance falls to 10.46 $\Omega$, the current rises to 0.5734 A, and the reading becomes $0.5734 \times 5.964 = 3.420$ V. (A1) The reading therefore decreases by about 0.009 V, which is 0.26%, because the voltmeter draws a small current that was not being drawn before. (A1)

(d) The power supplied by the cell is $P_{total} = EI = 6.0 \times 0.5714 = 3.429$ W. (M1) The power dissipated in the two resistors is $I^2(R_1+R_2) = (0.5714)^2(10.0) = 3.265$ W. (M1) The efficiency is therefore $3.265/3.429 = 0.952$, i.e. 95.2%. (A1) Equivalently, the efficiency is $\frac{R_1+R_2}{R_1+R_2+r} = \frac{10.0}{10.5}$, since the common factor $I^2$ cancels.

(e) With $R$ in place of $R_2$ the current is $I = \frac{E}{R + R_1 + r}$, so the power in $R$ is $P = I^2R = \frac{E^2R}{(R + 4.5)^2}$, writing $4.5$ for $R_1 + r$. (M1) Dividing numerator and denominator by $R$, $P = \frac{E^2}{R + 9.0 + 20.25/R}$, and the denominator is least when $R = 20.25/R$, that is $R = 4.5$ $\Omega$. (M1)(A1) The maximum power is $\frac{E^2}{4(R_1+r)} = \frac{36}{18.0} = 2.0$ W. (A1) Equivalently, $I = 6.0/9.0 = 0.667$ A and $P = (0.667)^2(4.5) = 2.0$ W.
questions.explanation:
The circuit is deliberately unremarkable: one cell, two resistors, one meter. The difficulty is entirely in keeping three different potential differences apart. The electromotive force of the cell is 6.0 V, the terminal potential difference is the e.m.f. minus the lost volts across the internal resistance, and the voltmeter reads neither of those, because it is connected across $R_2$ alone. With a current of 0.571 A the three are 6.00 V, 5.71 V and 3.43 V respectively, and the distractors in parts (a) and (b) are exactly the values a candidate gets by confusing them.

Part (c) is the part that separates a candidate who has met a real voltmeter from one who has only met an ideal one. Adding a resistance in parallel always lowers the resistance of the branch, so the total resistance falls, the current rises, and the potential difference across the parallel pair falls. The reading therefore decreases slightly. Because the voltmeter resistance of 1.0 k$\Omega$ is nearly two hundred times $R_2$, the change is only 0.26%, which is why an ideal voltmeter is a good approximation here and a poor one if $R_2$ were larger.

Part (d) has a shortcut worth seeing. Efficiency here is the fraction of the power that ends up in the external resistors rather than in the cell, and since every term in both powers carries a factor $I^2$, the current cancels and the efficiency is just the ratio of the external resistance to the total resistance, $10.0/10.5$. That is 95.2%, and it does not depend on the e.m.f. at all.

Part (e) asks for a maximum, not a value, so it cannot be answered by substituting into the equations already set up; the candidate has to decide what is varying. With $R$ as the variable, the power is $E^2R/(R+4.5)^2$, and the maximum falls at $R = 4.5$ $\Omega$, that is at $R_1 + r$. The result generalises: the power transferred to a load is greatest when the load resistance equals the resistance of everything else in the circuit. The maximum is 2.0 W, which is less than the 1.96 W + 1.31 W the two original resistors were dissipating between them, because the load here is a single resistor carrying the whole current.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.5 A potential divider designed from the unloaded ratio: the load appears in parallel with the lower resistor, the output falls by forty per cent, and with the upper resistor fixed the target output is an unattainable limit rather than a mistuning
questions.question:
A student is asked to design a circuit that delivers $4.00\ \mathrm{V}$ to a load of resistance $4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from a $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ supply of negligible internal resistance. She chooses a potential divider with a resistor $R_{1} = 8.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ in series with the supply and a resistor $R_{2} = 4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from the output to the negative terminal, and she checks the design with the load disconnected. The supply is then connected, the load is connected across $R_{2}$, and the output is measured. The load is purely resistive and its resistance does not change with temperature.

(a)

Calculate the potential difference across $R_{2}$ with the load disconnected, and state what fraction of the supply voltage that is.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the potential difference across the load once it is connected, and the current through $R_{1}$, through $R_{2}$ and through the load, showing that the currents are consistent.

[4]

(c)

Show that, with $R_{1}$ held at $8.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, no finite value of $R_{2}$ gives $4.00\ \mathrm{V}$ across this load, and state the value that the output approaches as $R_{2}$ is increased without limit.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate the design by calculating the fraction of the power drawn from the supply that reaches the load, and recommend one specific change that would allow the circuit to deliver $4.00\ \mathrm{V}$ to this load, supporting your recommendation with a calculation.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) With no load the two resistors are in series across the supply, so the current is $12.0/(8.0 + 4.0) = 1.00\ \mathrm{mA}$ and the potential difference across $R_{2}$ is (M1)
$$V_{\text{out}} = 12.0 \times \frac{4.0}{8.0 + 4.0} = 12.0 \times \frac{1}{3} = 4.00\ \mathrm{V} \;(A1),$$
which is one third of the supply voltage, in the same ratio as the two resistances (A1).
(b) With the load connected, $R_{2}$ and $R_{L}$ are in parallel (M1):
$$R_{p} = \frac{R_{2}R_{L}}{R_{2} + R_{L}} = \frac{4.0 \times 4.0}{4.0 + 4.0} = 2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega} \;(A1).$$
The total resistance of the circuit is now $8.0 + 2.0 = 10.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, so the current through $R_{1}$ is
$$I_{1} = \frac{12.0}{10.0 \times 10^{3}} = 1.20\ \mathrm{mA} \;(A1),$$
and the output falls to
$$V_{\text{out}} = 12.0 \times \frac{2.0}{8.0 + 2.0} = 2.40\ \mathrm{V},$$
a drop of forty per cent from the designed value (A1). The current splits equally between $R_{2}$ and the load, since both are $4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ at the same potential difference: $I_{2} = I_{L} = 2.40/4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega} = 0.60\ \mathrm{mA}$, and $0.60 + 0.60 = 1.20\ \mathrm{mA} = I_{1}$, as Kirchhoff's first law requires.
(c) For the output to be $4.00\ \mathrm{V}$ with $R_{1} = 8.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ and a supply of $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$, the divider ratio must be one third, which requires the parallel combination to satisfy (M1)
$$\frac{R_{p}}{8.0 + R_{p}} = \frac{1}{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 3R_{p} = 8.0 + R_{p} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_{p} = 4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega} \;(A1).$$
But $R_{p} = \dfrac{R_{2} \times 4.0}{R_{2} + 4.0}$ with $R_{2}$ in kilohms, and setting this equal to $4.0$ gives $4.0R_{2} = 4.0R_{2} + 16$, which is false for every value of $R_{2}$ (A1). The equation has no finite solution because the parallel combination of a $4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ load with any finite resistance is strictly less than $4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$: it approaches $4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from below as $R_{2} \to \infty$, and reaches it only in that limit. So the output approaches $4.00\ \mathrm{V}$ as $R_{2}$ is made larger and larger, but never attains it; at $R_{2} = 8.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ it is $3.00\ \mathrm{V}$, at $40\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ it is $3.75\ \mathrm{V}$, and at $400\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ it is $3.97\ \mathrm{V}$. The specification is unreachable with this $R_{1}$, not merely mistuned.
(d) The power delivered to the load is $V^{2}/R_{L} = 2.40^{2}/4.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega} = 1.44\ \mathrm{mW}$, and the power drawn from the supply is $\varepsilon I_{1} = 12.0 \times 1.20\ \mathrm{mA} = 14.4\ \mathrm{mW}$ (M1), so the fraction reaching the load is
$$\frac{1.44}{14.4} = 0.10 \;(A1).$$
Nine tenths of the power is dissipated in the two resistors of the divider, which is the penalty for choosing divider resistors comparable with the load. The remedy is to make both divider resistors small compared with the load, so that the load draws only a small fraction of the divider current. Keeping the one-third ratio and choosing $R_{2} = 2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ gives $R_{p} = 1.33\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, and the upper resistor must then be $R_{1} = 2R_{p} = 2.67\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ (A1):
$$V_{\text{out}} = 12.0 \times \frac{1.33}{2.67 + 1.33} = 4.00\ \mathrm{V}.$$
The load is then twice $R_{2}$ rather than equal to it, and the loading error is smaller by the same factor. An alternative acceptable answer is to keep the divider and insert a buffer amplifier, or to replace the divider with a voltage regulator; both remove the dependence of the output on the load rather than reducing it.
questions.explanation:
The potential divider is the first circuit most students learn to design, and the rule they learn is that the output voltage divides in the ratio of the two resistors. The rule is correct and it is stated in every textbook, and it is also the reason this design fails, because the rule holds only while nothing is connected to the output. As soon as a load draws current, the lower resistor and the load are in parallel, the effective lower resistance falls, and the divider ratio changes. The output does not sag slightly; it falls by forty per cent.

The reason the fall is so large is that the load resistance is equal to the lower resistor. Two equal resistors in parallel give half the resistance, so the lower arm of the divider is halved and the ratio changes from one third to one fifth. If the load were a hundred times the lower resistor, the parallel combination would be within one per cent of the lower resistor and the design would work. The whole question is the ratio of the load to the divider resistors, and the design as drawn ignores it.

Part (c) is the part that turns a numerical error into a structural one. It is tempting to think that a larger lower resistor would fix the sag, and up to a point it does: the output climbs from 2.40 V towards 4.00 V as the lower resistor grows. But it climbs towards a limit it cannot reach, because the parallel combination of the load with any finite resistor is less than the load resistance itself, and the required parallel combination is exactly equal to the load resistance. The equation that expresses the requirement has no solution, and seeing that is different from seeing that a particular value is wrong.

The efficiency calculation is the practical close. Ten per cent of the power reaches the load and ninety per cent is burnt in the divider, which is what happens when the divider's own resistances are of the same order as the load. The fix is not to tune the divider but to change its impedance level, and the calculation in part (d) shows the same one-third ratio realised with resistors that are small compared with the load.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.3 A hot-air balloon treated as a body immersed in the surrounding air: the density of the hot air is set by the absolute temperature, the temperature needed for a stated payload follows from the required density, and the payload has an upper bound equal to the mass of air displaced because the density of the hot air cannot fall below zero
questions.command_term: Show that, Determine, Show that, Comment
questions.question:
A hot-air balloon consists of an open envelope of volume $2200\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$ and a basket, whose combined mass, including the burner and the fuel, is $180\ \mathrm{kg}$. The envelope is open at the bottom, so the pressure of the air inside is equal to the pressure of the air outside. The outside air is at $288\ \mathrm{K}$ and a pressure of $1.01 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, and its molar mass is $0.0290\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}$. Take the gas constant as $R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The air inside the envelope is heated by the burner to a temperature $T$ and behaves as an ideal gas with the same molar mass. The balloon carries a payload of mass $m$ in addition to the mass of the envelope and basket. The volume of the envelope is taken as constant; the fabric does not stretch appreciably as the air inside is heated.

(a)

Show that the density of the outside air is $1.22\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and state why the density of the air inside the envelope at temperature $T$ is $1.22 \times \dfrac{288}{T}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

[3]

(b)

Determine the minimum temperature $T$ of the air inside the envelope required to lift a payload of $400\ \mathrm{kg}$, giving your answer in kelvin and in degrees Celsius.

[4]

(c)

Show that the payload has an upper bound that does not depend on the temperature of the air inside the envelope, and determine that bound.

[3]

(d)

A larger burner is fitted, doubling the temperature of the air inside the envelope above the value found in part (b). Determine the payload that this would allow, and comment on the claim that a sufficiently powerful burner could lift a payload of $3000\ \mathrm{kg}$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For a gas of molar mass $M$ the density is $\rho = pM/(RT)$ (M1), so
$$\rho_{\text{out}} = \frac{1.01 \times 10^{5} \times 0.0290}{8.31 \times 288} = \frac{2929}{2393} = 1.22\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} \;(A1).$$
Inside the envelope the pressure is the same as outside, because the envelope is open at the bottom, and the molar mass is the same. So the ratio of the densities is
$$\frac{\rho_{\text{in}}}{\rho_{\text{out}}} = \frac{pM/(RT)}{pM/(R \times 288)} = \frac{288}{T} \;(A1),$$
