and hence $\rho_{\text{in}} = 1.22 \times 288/T$ with $T$ in kelvin. The relation is between absolute temperatures: using degrees Celsius here would be meaningless, since the ratio $288/T$ would change with the zero of the scale.
(b) The upward force on the balloon is the weight of the air it displaces less the weight of the hot air inside, and for the balloon to lift a total mass $m_{\text{tot}}$ that force must at least balance the weight of that mass (M1):
$$(\rho_{\text{out}} - \rho_{\text{in}})Vg = m_{\text{tot}}g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \rho_{\text{in}} = \rho_{\text{out}} - \frac{m_{\text{tot}}}{V} \;(A1).$$
With $m_{\text{tot}} = 180 + 400 = 580\ \mathrm{kg}$,
$$\rho_{\text{in}} \le 1.22 - \frac{580}{2200} = 1.22 - 0.264 = 0.960\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} \;(A1),$$
and from part (a), $T = 288 \times \dfrac{1.22}{0.960} = 367\ \mathrm{K}$, that is $367 - 273 = 94\ \mathrm{{}^{\circ}C}$ (A1). This is comfortably within the range of a propane burner.
(c) The bound follows from part (b) without any new physics. Since the density of the air inside is $\rho_{\text{in}} = 1.22 \times 288/T$ and $T$ is an absolute temperature, $T > 0$ always, so $\rho_{\text{in}} > 0$ always (M1). The lift per unit volume is $\rho_{\text{out}} - \rho_{\text{in}}$, and it is largest when $\rho_{\text{in}}$ is smallest, which happens as $T \to \infty$ and $\rho_{\text{in}} \to 0$ (A1). So the greatest lift available is $\rho_{\text{out}}Vg$, the weight of the air displaced, and the greatest total mass that can be carried is
$$m_{\text{max}} = \rho_{\text{out}}V = 1.22 \times 2200 = 2692\ \mathrm{kg} \;(A1),$$
of which $180\ \mathrm{kg}$ is the balloon itself, leaving a maximum payload of about $2510\ \mathrm{kg}$. No burner, however powerful, can exceed this, because the envelope cannot displace more air than its own volume and the hot air inside always has some mass.
(d) Doubling the inside temperature from $367\ \mathrm{K}$ gives $T = 734\ \mathrm{K}$, and the inside density becomes
$$\rho_{\text{in}} = 1.22 \times \frac{288}{734} = 0.480\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} \;(M1).$$
The lift is then $(1.22 - 0.480) \times 2200 = 1636\ \mathrm{kg}$, so the payload is $1636 - 180 = 1456\ \mathrm{kg}$ (A1). Doubling the absolute temperature from 367 K to 734 K has raised the payload from 400 kg to 1456 kg, which is more than a doubling but far from unlimited; 734 K is $461\ \mathrm{{}^{\circ}C}$, hot enough to threaten most envelope fabrics, and it has bought less than four times the original payload.
The claim that a $3000\ \mathrm{kg}$ payload could be lifted is false, and part (c) says why before any calculation is attempted: $3000\ \mathrm{kg}$ exceeds the $2510\ \mathrm{kg}$ bound. If the required density is computed anyway it comes out negative, $\rho_{\text{in}} = 1.22 - 3000/2200 = -0.14\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and substituting that into $T = 288 \rho_{\text{out}}/\rho_{\text{in}}$ gives a negative absolute temperature, which is physically impossible (A1). A negative density is not a very hot gas; it is a sign that the equation has been asked for an answer that does not exist.
questions.explanation:
The physics here is a balance between two masses: the mass of the cold air the envelope pushes out of the way, and the mass of the hot air it contains. Everything else is bookkeeping. The balloon floats when the first exceeds the second plus the mass of everything hanging from it, and the only thing the burner does is reduce the second.

The relation that makes the problem solvable is that the envelope is open at the bottom. That single fact does two things: it fixes the pressure inside at the outside pressure, and it lets hot air escape as it expands, so the volume stays at 2200 cubic metres and the density falls. With the pressure and molar mass the same inside and out, the densities are in the inverse ratio of the absolute temperatures, and the temperature is the only variable the pilot controls.

Part (b) is the ordinary calculation and it is worth doing carefully, because the balloon itself counts. The payload is 400 kg but the mass to be lifted is 580 kg, and forgetting the 180 kg gives a required density of 1.042 rather than 0.960 and a temperature of 338 K rather than 367 K. The error is not large and it is in the direction of a balloon that will not leave the ground.

Part (c) is where the item stops being arithmetic. The density of the hot air is proportional to the reciprocal of the absolute temperature, and a reciprocal never reaches zero. So the lift saturates: it approaches the weight of the displaced air and stops. The number is 2692 kg of air displaced, of which 180 kg is the balloon, leaving about 2510 kg. That is a hard ceiling and it comes from the geometry of the envelope, not from the burner.

Part (d) makes the ceiling concrete. Doubling the absolute temperature from 367 K to 734 K is a real engineering achievement, and it raises the payload from 400 kg to about 1456 kg -- a large gain, but the last stretch towards the ceiling is enormously expensive, because the density falls only as $1/T$ while the temperature climbs. The request for 3000 kg is not difficult; it is impossible, and the negative density that comes out of the equation is the arithmetic telling the candidate so. Recognising that before computing is the point of asking part (c) first.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.4 Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends
questions.question:
A string of length 1.20 m and mass 3.60 g is fixed at both ends and set vibrating by a small oscillator attached at one end. The figure shows the mode of vibration that is produced when the oscillator is driven at 240 Hz. The string is under tension and vibrates in the plane of the page. The mass of the string is small compared with the masses that maintain the tension, so the tension may be taken as constant. Answer all parts with reference to the figure, and give numerical answers to three significant figures.

(a)

Determine the wavelength of the waves travelling along the string in this mode of vibration.

[2]

(b)

Calculate the speed of the transverse waves travelling along the string.

[2]

(c)

Calculate the tension in the string, stating the value of the mass per unit length that you use.

[3]

(d)

Determine the frequency of the fundamental mode of this string.

[2]

(e)

The oscillator frequency is now changed to 320 Hz while the tension is kept the same. Determine the harmonic that is produced, and explain why this frequency, and no neighbouring frequency, can produce a standing wave on this string.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The string is fixed at both ends, so both ends must be nodes and the length of the string must contain a whole number of half-wavelengths. (M1) Counting the antinodes in the figure gives three, so the string holds three half-wavelengths and $3\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) = 1.20$ m. Therefore $\lambda = \frac{2 \times 1.20}{3} = 0.800$ m. (A1) The nodes lie at the two ends and at 0.400 m and 0.800 m from one end, which is what the figure shows.

(b) The wave equation for a travelling wave is $v = f\lambda$, and the frequency of the standing wave equals the frequency of the travelling waves that compose it, so $v = 240 \times 0.800 = 192$ m s$^{-1}$. (M1)(A1) This is the speed at which a disturbance travels along the string, not the speed of any material point of the string, whose motion is transverse and much slower.

(c) The mass per unit length of the string is $\mu = \frac{m}{L} = \frac{3.60 \times 10^{-3}}{1.20} = 3.00 \times 10^{-3}$ kg m$^{-1}$. (M1) For a stretched string the wave speed is related to the tension by $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, so $T = \mu v^2$. (M1) Substituting, $T = (3.00 \times 10^{-3})(192)^2 = (3.00 \times 10^{-3})(3.6864 \times 10^4) = 111$ N. (A1) A tension of about a hundred newtons is plausible for a string weighing a few grams, which is a useful check on the arithmetic.

(d) The fundamental mode is the longest wavelength the string can support, with a single antinode and one half-wavelength across the fixed length. (M1) Hence $\lambda_1 = 2L = 2.40$ m and $f_1 = \frac{v}{\lambda_1} = \frac{192}{2.40} = 80.0$ Hz. (A1) Equivalently, the mode shown is the third harmonic, so $f_1 = \frac{240}{3} = 80.0$ Hz, and the two routes must agree.

(e) The standing waves possible on a string fixed at both ends have frequencies $f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}$, which are the integer multiples of the fundamental 80.0 Hz. (M1) Since $\frac{320}{80.0} = 4$ exactly, the driving frequency coincides with the fourth harmonic, so a standing wave with four half-wavelengths and four antinodes is produced. (A1) At any other frequency the waves reflected from the fixed ends return out of phase with the driver. (M1) The reflected wave then interferes destructively at the driver instead of reinforcing it, so the amplitude does not build up and only a small forced vibration remains. (A1) Resonance requires the round trip along the string to be a whole number of wavelengths, which is exactly the condition that the driving frequency be a harmonic; a frequency a few hertz away would leave the string forced but not resonant.
questions.explanation:
The figure gives the shape of a mode, not a measurement, so the first thing to do is to read it as a boundary-condition statement. Both ends are fixed, so both are nodes, and the number of half-wavelengths that fit between them is an integer. Counting the antinodes in the figure gives three, so the string holds three half-wavelengths, and since the string is 1.20 m long each half-wavelength is 0.400 m and the wavelength is 0.800 m. A candidate who reads three wavelengths instead of three half-wavelengths gets 0.400 m, which then makes the speed wrong by a factor of two.

With the wavelength and the driving frequency the wave equation gives the speed immediately, and with the speed and the linear density it gives the tension. The linear density is where the units do the damage: the string has a mass of 3.60 g, which is $3.60 \times 10^{-3}$ kg, and dividing by 1.20 m gives $3.00 \times 10^{-3}$ kg m$^{-1}$. Using grams throughout gives a tension a hundred thousand times too large, which is the sort of answer a candidate should notice is absurd for a string.

Part (d) reverses the harmonic series. The mode that is drawn is the third harmonic at 240 Hz, so the fundamental is 240/3 = 80.0 Hz, and the string can vibrate at 80, 160, 240, 320 Hz and so on.

Part (e) is the conceptual centre of the item. The temptation is to assume that a string driven at any frequency will vibrate at that frequency, which is true of the forced vibration but not of the standing wave. A standing wave requires the waves reflected from the ends to return in phase with the driver, and that happens only when the round-trip path length is a whole number of wavelengths. Here 320 Hz is exactly four times the fundamental, so it is the fourth harmonic and a standing wave with four antinodes appears. A frequency of 310 Hz would force the string to move, but the reflected waves would arrive out of phase, the amplitude would not build up, and no stable standing wave would form.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.2 A pulley with a non-negligible moment of inertia, and why the two tensions differ
questions.command_term: Show that, Determine, Explain, Show that
questions.question:
A block of mass $m_{1} = 2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ hangs vertically from a light inextensible string. The string passes over a pulley and is attached to a second block of mass $m_{2} = 3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ resting on a horizontal frictionless table. The pulley is a uniform solid disc of mass $M = 1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $r = 0.10\ \mathrm{m}$, free to rotate about a fixed horizontal axis through its centre. The string does not slip on the pulley. Take $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(a)

By applying Newton's second law to each block and the rotational form of the second law to the pulley, show that the acceleration of the blocks is $a = 3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ to two significant figures.

[3]

(b)

Determine the tension in the string on the hanging-block side and the tension on the table side, each to three significant figures.

[4]

(c)

Explain, referring to a torque, why the two tensions are not equal even though the string is light and does not slip.

[3]

(d)

The hanging block falls through $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Show that the energy lost by the falling block equals the sum of the translational and rotational kinetic energies gained.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) Let the tension on the hanging side be $T_{1}$ and on the table side $T_{2}$, and let the blocks accelerate at $a$.

For the hanging block, taking downwards as positive (M1):
$$m_{1}g - T_{1} = m_{1}a$$

For the table block, the only horizontal force is $T_{2}$ (M1):
$$T_{2} = m_{2}a$$

The pulley is a uniform solid disc, so $I = \tfrac{1}{2}Mr^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.0)(0.10)^{2} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}$ (A1).

Because the string does not slip, $\alpha = a/r$, and the net torque on the pulley is $(T_{1} - T_{2})r$:
$$(T_{1} - T_{2})r = I\alpha = I\frac{a}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{1} - T_{2} = \frac{I}{r^{2}}a$$

Substituting $I = \tfrac{1}{2}Mr^{2}$ gives $T_{1} - T_{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}Ma$. Adding this to the two block equations eliminates both tensions (M1):
$$m_{1}g = \left(m_{1} + m_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}M\right)a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a = \frac{m_{1}g}{m_{1} + m_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}M}$$

Numerically $\tfrac{1}{2}M = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$, so
$$a = \frac{(2.0)(9.81)}{2.0 + 3.0 + 0.50} = \frac{19.62}{5.50} = 3.57\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \tag{AG}$$

(b) From the hanging block (M1)(A1):
$$T_{1} = m_{1}(g - a) = 2.0\,(9.81 - 3.567) = 12.5\ \mathrm{N}$$

From the table block (M1)(A1):
$$T_{2} = m_{2}a = 3.0 \times 3.567 = 10.7\ \mathrm{N}$$

The difference is $T_{1} - T_{2} = 1.78\ \mathrm{N}$.

(c) The pulley is not in translational equilibrium in the rotational sense: it must gain angular speed at rate $\alpha = a/r = 35.7\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}$, and a body with moment of inertia needs a net torque to do that. The two tensions act on opposite sides of the axis, so their torques oppose; only their difference is left over to accelerate the pulley. If the tensions were equal the net torque would be zero and the pulley could never start turning. Because the string does not slip, the pulley must turn as the blocks move, so a non-zero net torque is unavoidable and the tensions cannot be equal.

(d) Energy lost by the falling block:
$$m_{1}gh = 2.0 \times 9.81 \times 1.0 = 19.6\ \mathrm{J}$$

Speed after falling $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from rest: $v^{2} = 2ah = 2(3.567)(1.0) = 7.13\ \mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-2}}$, so $v = 2.67\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Translational kinetic energy:
$$\tfrac{1}{2}(m_{1} + m_{2})v^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(5.0)(7.13) = 17.8\ \mathrm{J}$$

Rotational kinetic energy, with $\omega = v/r = 26.7\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$:
$$\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(5.0 \times 10^{-3})(26.7)^{2} = 1.78\ \mathrm{J}$$

The sum is $17.8 + 1.78 = 19.6\ \mathrm{J}$, equal to the energy lost by the falling block (AG). The rotational term is exactly the $\tfrac{1}{2}M$ in the denominator of part (a): the pulley's share of the energy is the reason the acceleration is smaller than the ideal-pulley value.
questions.explanation:
The discriminating move is recognising that a pulley with mass breaks the assumption every introductory treatment makes: that the tension is uniform along a light string. Here the string is light and inextensible, so the temptation is to carry the ideal-string result over and set $T_{1} = T_{2}$. That is the single most common error, and it is worth about ten per cent of the acceleration, which is large enough to be visible but small enough to look plausible on a calculator.

The physical content is that the pulley is a body with moment of inertia that must acquire angular speed, and the only torques available are the two tension torques, which oppose. Their difference is what remains. The cleanest route is to write the three equations and add them, which makes the cancellation of the tensions obvious and yields the effective mass $\tfrac{1}{2}M$ in the denominator. That $\tfrac{1}{2}M$ has a direct energy meaning, which is exactly what part (d) is for: the pulley stores $1.78\ \mathrm{J}$ of rotational kinetic energy out of the $19.6\ \mathrm{J}$ released, and that share is why the blocks accelerate more slowly than they would with an ideal pulley.

Part (c) is where a student who has merely memorised a formula is separated from one who has understood it. There is no equation to write; the answer is a statement about the necessity of a net torque. Part (d) then closes the loop, because the energy that "disappeared" from the blocks reappears in the pulley's rotation. A candidate who finds the three energies do not balance has usually used $I = Mr^{2}$ instead of $\tfrac{1}{2}Mr^{2}$ and should be sent back to the definition of the moment of inertia for a disc.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.4 Efficiency of a rectangular pV cycle, and why the Carnot value is not the answer
questions.question:
A fixed mass of ideal monatomic gas is taken round the closed cycle A$\rightarrow$B$\rightarrow$C$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$A shown in the table of states. The gas has molar heat capacities $C_{V} = \tfrac{3}{2}R$ and $C_{P} = \tfrac{5}{2}R$ and behaves ideally throughout.

| State | $p\,/\,10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ | $V\,/\,10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$ |
|---|---|---|
| A | 3.0 | 1.0 |
| B | 3.0 | 3.0 |
| C | 1.0 | 3.0 |
| D | 1.0 | 1.0 |

A$\rightarrow$B is isobaric, B$\rightarrow$C is isochoric, C$\rightarrow$D is isobaric and D$\rightarrow$A is isochoric.

(a)

Determine the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle, and state how this follows from the shape of the cycle on a $pV$ diagram.

[3]

(b)

Determine the total thermal energy supplied to the gas during the cycle, taking care to identify which legs supply energy rather than remove it.

[4]

(c)

Calculate the thermal efficiency of the cycle, and calculate the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the highest and lowest temperatures reached by this gas.

[3]

(d)

Explain why the Carnot value cannot be the efficiency of this cycle, however ideal the gas.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) On a $pV$ diagram the work done in a cycle is the area enclosed. The cycle is a rectangle spanning $\Delta p = 2.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $\Delta V = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$ (M1), so
$$W = \Delta p\,\Delta V = (2.0 \times 10^{5})(2.0 \times 10^{-3}) = 400\ \mathrm{J} \tag{A1}$$

The cycle is traced clockwise, so the gas does net work on the surroundings; the isochoric legs contribute nothing because $\Delta V = 0$ (R1).

(b) Because $pV \propto T$, the four states have $pV$ products in the ratio $300 : 900 : 300 : 100$ in units of $\mathrm{J}$.

On the isobaric legs $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}\Delta(pV)$ and on the isochoric legs $Q = \tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(pV)$:

A$\rightarrow$B: $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}(900 - 300) = +1500\ \mathrm{J}$ (M1)(A1)
B$\rightarrow$C: $Q = \tfrac{3}{2}(300 - 900) = -900\ \mathrm{J}$
C$\rightarrow$D: $Q = \tfrac{5}{2}(100 - 300) = -500\ \mathrm{J}$
D$\rightarrow$A: $Q = \tfrac{3}{2}(300 - 100) = +300\ \mathrm{J}$ (M1)

The legs that supply energy are A$\rightarrow$B and D$\rightarrow$A, so
$$Q_{\mathrm{in}} = 1500 + 300 = 1800\ \mathrm{J} \tag{A1}$$

The check that the bookkeeping is right: the signed sum is $1500 - 900 - 500 + 300 = +400\ \mathrm{J}$, which is exactly $W$ from part (a), as the first law requires for a cycle.

(c) Thermal efficiency (M1)(A1):
$$\eta = \frac{W}{Q_{\mathrm{in}}} = \frac{400}{1800} = 0.222 = 22.2\ \%$$

Highest and lowest temperatures: $pV$ is greatest at B ($900$) and least at D ($100$), so the Carnot bound is (M1)
$$\eta_{C} = 1 - \frac{T_{D}}{T_{B}} = 1 - \frac{100}{900} = 0.889 = 88.9\ \%$$

(d) The Carnot efficiency is the bound for a cycle made of two isothermal and two adiabatic legs, which is the most efficient cycle possible between two reservoirs. This cycle has no isothermal legs at all: A$\rightarrow$B and C$\rightarrow$D are isobaric and B$\rightarrow$C and D$\rightarrow$A are isochoric. Heat is therefore transferred across a continuously changing temperature range rather than at two fixed temperatures, and part of the heat transfer is irreversible. The Carnot expression is an upper bound that this cycle does not approach, and quoting it as the answer confuses the bound with the value.
questions.explanation:
The trap is the presence of a memorable formula that fits the shape of the question but not its content. Given a cycle with a hot and a cold extreme, $1 - T_{c}/T_{h}$ is the first thing a prepared student reaches for, and here it returns $88.9\ \%$ against a true value of $22.2\ \%$. The two numbers are far enough apart that a student who checks the result against the first law will notice, which is the point: the item rewards checking and punishes pattern-matching.

The real work is in part (b). Efficiency is $W/Q_{\mathrm{in}}$, and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}$ is not the sum of the four heat terms, two of which are negative. Identifying which legs supply heat is the discriminating step: A$\rightarrow$B and D$\rightarrow$A, both of which raise $pV$. A candidate who sums the magnitudes, or who uses the net heat, gets a different denominator and therefore a different efficiency. Part (a) is placed first precisely so that the student has $W = 400\ \mathrm{J}$ in hand and can use the cyclic identity $\sum Q = W$ to check part (b); that identity is exact here and catches the error immediately.

Part (d) asks for the reason rather than the rule. The Carnot efficiency is the efficiency of a specific cycle, not a general bound that any cycle approaches; the gap here is large because the isobaric legs transfer heat across a range of temperatures, and the isochoric legs transfer heat with no work at all. Understanding that the bound is unattainable without the two isothermal legs is the difference between knowing a formula and knowing what it is for.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.2 Intensity and intensity level from a point source, and adding a second source
questions.question:
A small loudspeaker radiates sound uniformly in all directions and may be treated as a point source emitting a total acoustic power of $P = 0.50\ \mathrm{W}$. Take the threshold of hearing as $I_{0} = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and the intensity level as $L = 10\log_{10}(I/I_{0})$.

(a)

Calculate the intensity of the sound at a distance of $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from the loudspeaker.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the intensity level at that distance, in decibels.

[3]

(c)

A second, identical loudspeaker is placed at the same position and emits the same power. The two sources are incoherent. Determine the new intensity level, and state the increase in decibels.

[3]

(d)

Determine the distance from the single loudspeaker at which the intensity level is $90\ \mathrm{dB}$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) A point source spreads its power over a sphere of area $4\pi r^{2}$ (M1), so
$$I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^{2}} = \frac{0.50}{4\pi (2.0)^{2}} = \frac{0.50}{50.3} = 9.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} \tag{A1}$$

The area is $4\pi(2.0)^{2} = 50.3\ \mathrm{m^{2}}$ (A1).

(b) The ratio to the threshold is
$$\frac{I}{I_{0}} = \frac{9.947 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-12}} = 9.9 \times 10^{9} \quad\text{(M1)}$$

$$L = 10\log_{10}(9.9 \times 10^{9}) = 10 \times 9.997 = 100\ \mathrm{dB} \tag{A1(A1)}$$

so $L \approx 1.0 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{dB}$ to two significant figures.

(c) Intensities of incoherent sources add, so the new intensity is $2I$ (M1):
$$I' = 2 \times 9.947 \times 10^{-3} = 1.99 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$$

$$L' = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{2I}{I_{0}}\right) = 10\log_{10}2 + 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right) = 3.01 + 99.98 = 103\ \mathrm{dB} \tag{A1}$$

The increase is therefore
$$\Delta L = 10\log_{10}2 = 3.0\ \mathrm{dB} \tag{A1}$$

Doubling the acoustic power adds a fixed $3.0\ \mathrm{dB}$, whatever the original level.

(d) The level falls by $20\log_{10}(r/r_{1})$ when the distance increases from $r_{1}$ to $r$, because the intensity falls as $1/r^{2}$ and the logarithm brings down a factor of two (M1). Requiring $L = 90\ \mathrm{dB}$:
$$99.98 - 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{r}{2.0}\right) = 90 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{r}{2.0}\right) = 9.98$$

$$\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{r}{2.0}\right) = 0.499 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{r}{2.0} = 3.16 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = 6.3\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1(A1)}$$

Check: at $6.3\ \mathrm{m}$, $I = 0.50/(4\pi \times 39.7) = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, which is $10^{9}I_{0}$ and gives exactly $90\ \mathrm{dB}$.

Two results from this question are worth carrying away. Doubling the power of an incoherent source adds exactly three decibels whatever the starting level, because what doubles is the intensity and the level is logarithmic in intensity. And the level falls by about six decibels for every doubling of the distance from a point source, because the intensity falls by a factor of four and ten times the logarithm of four is six. Those two numbers between them cover most of the practical reasoning about sound levels, and neither can be reached without going through the intensity.
questions.explanation:
Two separate traps are laid here, and they fail in opposite directions. The first is that sound levels do not add: two identical sources at $100\ \mathrm{dB}$ produce $103\ \mathrm{dB}$, not $200\ \mathrm{dB}$, because the decibel scale is logarithmic and what doubles is the intensity. This is the single most commonly misremembered fact in the whole topic, and the number $200$ is so obviously wrong to anyone who has stood next to two loudspeakers that it is a useful self-check.

The second trap is the factor in front of the logarithm. Intensity level is defined with a factor of $10$, so an intensity ratio of $10^{9}$ is $90\ \mathrm{dB}$. Distance, however, enters through $20\log_{10}(r)$, not $10\log_{10}(r)$, because the intensity depends on $r^{2}$ and the logarithm of a square is twice the logarithm. A student who carries the factor $10$ across from the level definition gets $20\ \mathrm{m}$ instead of $6.3\ \mathrm{m}$ in the final part, an error of a factor of three that is easy to make and easy to miss.

The question is sequenced so that the student has to move in both directions across the logarithmic bridge: forward in (b), where an intensity becomes a level, and backward in (d), where a level becomes a distance. Part (c) sits between them and tests the one rule that cannot be applied by pattern: that superposition of intensities is linear but superposition of levels is not.

The self-check built into the last line of part (d) is deliberate. A student who finds a distance of about six metres can put it back into the inverse-square law and recover ninety decibels exactly, which confirms the factor of twenty without having to trust it. That is the habit the question is trying to install: a logarithmic result is easy to get wrong by a constant factor, and the constant factor is always visible if the answer is substituted back.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme D: Fields
questions.subtopic: D.2 A charged oil drop held at rest, and the p.d. that gives it an upward acceleration
questions.question:
Two large horizontal parallel plates are separated by $d = 12\ \mathrm{mm}$ and connected to a variable power supply. A small oil drop of mass $m = 3.27 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{kg}$ carries a charge $q$ and is observed to remain stationary between the plates when the potential difference is $V = 480\ \mathrm{V}$. Take $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and the elementary charge as $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. The drop may be treated as a point charge and air resistance is negligible.

(a)

Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength between the plates.

[3]

(b)

Determine the magnitude of the charge on the drop, and hence determine how many elementary charges it carries.

[4]

(c)

The potential difference is now adjusted so that the drop accelerates upwards with an acceleration of magnitude $g$. Determine the new potential difference, using your value of $q$ from part (b).

[3]

(d)

State one assumption made in treating the drop as stationary in equilibrium, and say how the answer to (b) would change if that assumption failed.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) The field between parallel plates is uniform, so (M1)(A1)
$$E = \frac{V}{d} = \frac{480}{12 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$$

with the field directed downwards if the upper plate is positive (A1).

(b) For the drop to be stationary the electric force must balance the weight exactly (M1):
$$qE = mg \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = \frac{mg}{E} = \frac{(3.27 \times 10^{-15})(9.81)}{4.0 \times 10^{4}}$$

$$q = \frac{3.208 \times 10^{-14}}{4.0 \times 10^{4}} = 8.02 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C} \tag{A1}$$

The number of elementary charges (M1):
$$n = \frac{q}{e} = \frac{8.02 \times 10^{-19}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.01 \approx 5 \tag{A1}$$

The charge is $5e$, so the drop carries five excess electrons (or lacks five electrons, depending on the sign chosen).

(c) An upward acceleration of magnitude $g$ requires a net upward force equal to $mg$, so the electric force must be $2mg$ (M1):
$$qE' = 2mg \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E' = \frac{2mg}{q}$$

But $mg/q = E = 4.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ from part (b), so
$$E' = 2E = 8.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}} \tag{A1}$$

$$V' = E'd = (8.0 \times 10^{4})(12 \times 10^{-3}) = 9.6 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{V} \tag{A1}$$

(d) The assumption is that the only forces are the electric force and the weight, so buoyancy and drag are negligible. If the drop also experienced an upward buoyant force $F_{b}$, the electric force required for equilibrium would be smaller, $qE = mg - F_{b}$, and the charge deduced in (b) would come out too small; the value of $n$ would then be less than $5$ and would no longer be an integer.

Part (c) can be seen without any arithmetic once the structure is clear. Equilibrium required the electric force to equal the weight, and an upward acceleration of magnitude $g$ requires a net force equal to the weight, so the electric force has to supply one weight to hold the drop up and a second weight to accelerate it. It must therefore double, and so must the field and the potential difference. The charge found in part (b) is then only needed to confirm the direction of the field, which is a useful reminder that a quantity can be known without being needed.
questions.explanation:
The item is a two-stage test of the same idea, and the second stage is where the marks are lost. In parts (a) and (b) the drop is stationary, so the electric force equals the weight and the charge follows from a straightforward balance. Almost every student who has met the Millikan experiment can do this, and the numbers are arranged so that the charge comes out at $5.01e$, close enough to an integer to be unmistakable but not so exact that it looks contrived.

Part (c) changes the question from "what force balances?" to "what force produces this acceleration?", and those are different questions. An upward acceleration of $g$ needs a net upward force of $mg$, so the electric force must supply $mg$ to hold the drop up and a further $mg$ to accelerate it, giving $2mg$ in total. The p.d. therefore doubles to $960\ \mathrm{V}$. The wrong answer is $480\ \mathrm{V}$, which is already printed in the question, and it is wrong for a specific and instructive reason: it satisfies the equilibrium condition that part (b) was about, and applying the earlier condition to a new question is exactly the habit this part is designed to detect.

Part (d) asks for an assumption and its consequence, which is a different kind of demand: it tests whether the student can see that "stationary" was a physical claim and not merely a description of the diagram. The most natural omission is buoyancy, and it is instructive that including it makes the deduced charge too small and destroys the integer, because that is precisely the kind of systematic error Millikan had to reason about. The item is arranged so that a student who understands the structure can see the answer to (c) without much arithmetic, and a student who does not will produce the number already given in the stem.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme D: Fields
questions.subtopic: D.3 A velocity selector, and the circular path of a singly and a doubly charged ion
questions.question:
A velocity selector consists of a region in which a uniform electric field of magnitude $E = 2.5 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B = 0.50\ \mathrm{T}$ are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of motion of a beam of ions. Ions that pass through undeflected then enter a second region containing only the same magnetic field, where they move in circular arcs.

(a)

Show that an ion passes through the crossed fields undeflected only if its speed is $v = E/B$, and calculate that speed.

[3]

(b)

A singly charged ion of mass $3.32 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}$ enters the second region with the speed found in (a). Determine the radius of its circular path.

[4]

(c)

A doubly charged ion of the same mass enters the second region at the same speed. Determine the radius of its path and compare it with the radius in (b).

[3]

(d)

Explain why the speed selected by the crossed fields does not depend on the mass or the charge of the ion.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) In the crossed fields the electric force $qE$ and the magnetic force $qvB$ act in opposite directions (M1). For the ion to pass undeflected the resultant must be zero:
$$qE = qvB \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \frac{E}{B} \tag{AG}$$

The charge cancels, so the condition is independent of $q$. Numerically (A1)(A1):
$$v = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{5}}{0.50} = 5.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

(b) In the second region the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it supplies the centripetal force (M1):
$$qvB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \frac{mv}{qB} \tag{A1}$$

With $q = e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ (M1):
$$r = \frac{(3.32 \times 10^{-26})(5.0 \times 10^{5})}{(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(0.50)} = \frac{1.66 \times 10^{-20}}{8.01 \times 10^{-20}} = 0.207\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1}$$

(c) For the doubly charged ion, $q = 2e$, so (M1)
$$r_{2} = \frac{mv}{2eB} = \frac{r}{2} = \frac{0.207}{2} = 0.104\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1}$$

The radius is exactly halved. The same speed and the same mass produce the same momentum, so doubling the charge doubles the centripetal force available and the ion curves twice as tightly (A1).

(d) The two forces in the selector are both proportional to the charge: the electric force is $qE$ and the magnetic force is $qvB$. Setting them equal divides the charge out, leaving $v = E/B$, which contains neither $q$ nor $m$. The selection is therefore a statement about speed alone, and ions of different mass and different charge all pass undeflected provided they are travelling at that one speed. This is what makes the device useful as the first stage of a mass spectrometer: it delivers a beam of known speed, so the radius in the second region can be interpreted as a measurement of $m/q$.

The halving in part (c) is exact rather than approximate, and that exactness is itself a check on the reasoning. Only one quantity changed, and the charge appears to the first power in the expression for the radius, so the radius must change by exactly the same factor. A student who obtains anything other than a clean factor of two has usually applied the magnetic force to the wrong region, or has forgotten that the force in the second region is the one supplying the centripetal acceleration.
questions.explanation:
The item is about a fact that is easy to state and easy to lose sight of: the velocity selector selects a speed and nothing else. Part (a) derives it, and the derivation is short, which is the point, because the charge cancels in the first line and the mass never appears at all. The two later parts then test whether that cancellation was understood rather than merely written down.

Part (c) is where the understanding is separated from the memorisation. A student who has learned $r = mv/(qB)$ as a formula will substitute $q = 2e$ and get the right answer, which is fine. A student who reasons physically, however, should notice that the momentum is unchanged and the available centripetal force has doubled, so the arc must be twice as tight. Both routes arrive at $0.104\ \mathrm{m}$, and the wrong answer, that the radius is unchanged because nothing about the motion changed, comes from treating the charge as a spectator when in fact it appears in both forces.

The second region also has a structural role. The ion arrives with a known speed, so measuring the radius measures $m/q$, and that is the whole principle of the mass spectrometer. Part (d) asks for the reason the first stage works at all, and the answer is a cancellation rather than a coincidence: both forces are proportional to the same charge, so their ratio is a property of the fields. The item deliberately gives a mass that is not a familiar particle mass, so that the student cannot shortcut the calculation by recognising the ion.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.2 Stopping potential against frequency, with one anomalous reading
questions.question:
The results are shown in the table. Einstein's photoelectric equation may be written $eV_{s} = hf - \phi$, where $V_{s}$ is the stopping potential and $\phi$ is the work function of the cathode.

(a)

State the quantity that should be plotted on the vertical axis so that the data give a straight line, and state what the gradient of that line represents.

[2]

(b)

Determine the gradient of the best-fit straight line through the reliable points, and hence determine a value for the Planck constant.

[3]

(c)

Calculate the threshold frequency and the work function of the cathode in electronvolts.

[3]

(d)

Identify the reading that is inconsistent with the rest, and justify your choice using a residual rather than by eye.

[2]

(e)

Suggest one experimental cause for that reading, and state what a repeat measurement would need to show for the reading to be accepted.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) Plot $V_{s}$ on the vertical axis against $f$ on the horizontal axis. Because $eV_{s} = hf - \phi$, this is linear, and comparing with $y = mx + c$ shows that the gradient is $h/e$, the Planck constant divided by the elementary charge. The intercept on the $V_{s}$ axis is $-\phi/e$.

(b) The five reliable points are at $f = 5.00, 6.00, 8.00, 9.00$ and $10.0$ in units of $10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, with $V_{s} = 0.57, 0.98, 1.81, 2.22$ and $2.64\ \mathrm{V}$.

For these five points $\sum f = 38.0$, $\sum V_{s} = 8.22$, $\sum f^{2} = 306$ and $\sum f V_{s} = 69.59$ (M1)(A1). Hence
$$m = \frac{5(69.59) - (38.0)(8.22)}{5(306) - (38.0)^{2}} = \frac{347.95 - 312.36}{1530 - 1444} = \frac{35.59}{86.0} = 0.414\ \mathrm{V\,per\,}10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$$

The gradient is $h/e$, so (M1)
$$h = \frac{m e}{10^{14}} = \frac{0.414 \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19}}{10^{14}} = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$$

which is within $0.1\ \%$ of the accepted value $6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$ (A1).

(c) The intercept is
$$c = \frac{\sum V_{s} - m\sum f}{5} = \frac{8.22 - 0.4138 \times 38.0}{5} = -1.50\ \mathrm{V}$$

The threshold frequency is where $V_{s} = 0$ (M1):
$$f_{0} = -\frac{c}{m} = \frac{1.50}{0.4138} = 3.63 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz} \tag{A1}$$

The work function is the energy of a photon at the threshold (M1):
$$\phi = hf_{0} = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.63 \times 10^{14}) = 2.41 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = \frac{2.41 \times 10^{-19}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.50\ \mathrm{eV} \tag{A1}$$

(d) The reading at $f = 7.00 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is inconsistent. Using $V_{s} = 0.4138f - 1.50$ in units of $10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, the residuals are $+0.002, -0.002, +0.354, +0.000, -0.003$ and $+0.003\ \mathrm{V}$ for the six points in order (M1). The residual at $7.00$ is $+0.354\ \mathrm{V}$, more than a hundred times the largest of the others and some seventeen times the $0.02\ \mathrm{V}$ repeatability of the measurements, so it cannot be explained by the scatter of the apparatus (A1).

(e) A likely cause is that the violet or blue source used for that point was not clean monochromatic light, or that the cathode surface had been contaminated or oxidised since the previous reading, which would raise the apparent work function locally and hence the stopping potential. Another possibility is that the reverse potential was adjusted too quickly and the photocurrent had not fallen fully to zero when the reading was taken.

A repeat measurement would need to reproduce the raised value with the same source and a freshly cleaned cathode, and the residual would need to fall within the same few millivolts as the other points, before the reading could be accepted as evidence of a real departure from the linear relation.
questions.explanation:
This item tests the whole experimental loop rather than a single formula: choose the linearising variable, fit the reliable data, extract two physical constants, and then account for the point that does not fit. The last of those is the discriminating step, because the natural instinct is to average all six points and report whatever comes out, which is exactly what makes the anomaly dangerous.

The anomalous reading at $7.00 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is raised by $0.35\ \mathrm{V}$ above the line defined by the other five. That is large: the stated repeatability is $0.02\ \mathrm{V}$, so the deviation is roughly seventeen times the measurement scatter, and it cannot be argued away as noise. Because it sits near the middle of the frequency range, it has real leverage on the fitted gradient, and including it lowers $h$ from $6.63$ to $6.47 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, an error of $2.4\ \%$ that is well outside the precision the other points support. The item is therefore arranged so that the careless route produces a visibly wrong constant, which is the strongest possible argument for looking at residuals.

Part (e) is deliberately open, but it is not free: the mark is for a cause with a mechanism and for a stated criterion for accepting the reading. The physically motivated answers all involve something that would raise the stopping potential for that one source, such as contamination of the cathode or a source that is not monochromatic. The part is there because a data-based question that only asks students to find the outlier teaches them to delete data; asking what would have to be true for the reading to be kept teaches them to test it.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.1 Ice added to warm water when the ice does not all melt
questions.question:
A student places $m_{\mathrm{ice}} = 0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice, initially at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, into $m_{w} = 0.200\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $10.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. Take the specific heat capacity of water as $c_{w} = 4180\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and the specific latent heat of fusion of ice as $L_{f} = 3.34 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

(a)

Calculate the thermal energy released when the water cools to $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

[2]

(b)

Calculate the thermal energy required to melt all of the ice at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

[2]

(c)

Determine the final temperature of the mixture, justifying the assumption you make about the ice.

[4]

(d)

Determine the mass of ice that remains unmelted at equilibrium, and state what has happened to the temperature of the original water.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Cooling the water from $10.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (M1)(A1):
$$Q_{\mathrm{avail}} = m_{w}c_{w}\Delta T = 0.200 \times 4180 \times 10.0 = 8.36 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$$

(b) Melting the whole $0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice at its melting point (M1)(A1):
$$Q_{\mathrm{need}} = m_{\mathrm{ice}}L_{f} = 0.050 \times 3.34 \times 10^{5} = 1.67 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$$

(c) Compare the two energies before doing anything else: $8.36 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$ is available and $1.67 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$ is needed, so only part of the ice can melt (R1). The mixture therefore settles at the melting point of ice, and the final temperature is
$$T_{f} = 0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \tag{A1}$$

The justification is that the water cannot cool below $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ while ice is still present: any further energy it released would have to come out of the ice, which is already at its melting point and cannot get colder without freezing (R1)(A1).

(d) All of the energy released by the water goes into melting ice at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so (M1):
$$m_{\mathrm{melted}} = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{avail}}}{L_{f}} = \frac{8.36 \times 10^{3}}{3.34 \times 10^{5}} = 0.0250\ \mathrm{kg} \tag{A1}$$

The ice remaining is
$$m_{\mathrm{left}} = 0.050 - 0.0250 = 0.0250\ \mathrm{kg} \tag{A1}$$

The original water has cooled all the way to $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and no further; it is now in equilibrium with ice at the melting point, so the mixture consists of $0.225\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water and $0.0250\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice, both at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

The wider lesson is worth stating plainly, because this is the part that generalises. A mixture of ice and water has two possible regimes, and the numbers decide which one applies rather than the student. If the warm body holds more energy than the fusion of all the ice requires, the ice melts completely and the final temperature follows from a single equation. If it holds less, the ice survives and the temperature is pinned at the melting point instead. The algebra of the first regime is the one everybody learns, and it is also the one that gives a nonsensical answer here, so the check has to come before the equation rather than after it.
questions.explanation:
This item tests whether a student tests an assumption or merely applies a formula. The familiar mixture problem has a fixed recipe: equate the heat lost by the warm body to the heat gained by the cold body, solve for $T_{f}$, done. That recipe contains a hidden premise, namely that the ice melts completely, and it is a premise that is usually true in textbook problems and false here.

The numbers are chosen so that the failure is unmistakable rather than marginal. Only $8.36\ \mathrm{kJ}$ is available while $16.7\ \mathrm{kJ}$ is needed, so the recipe produces a final temperature near $-8\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$: below the melting point of ice, in a container holding ice. A student who obtains that number and writes it down has produced a result that contradicts the data given, and the whole point of the question is whether the contradiction is noticed.

The correct reasoning is a two-line energy audit performed before any algebra: compare what is available with what is needed, conclude that the ice cannot all melt, and therefore conclude that the temperature is pinned at $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by the coexistence of ice and water. The temperature is then not something to be calculated at all; it is fixed by the physics, and the actual calculation is the mass of ice consumed. Part (d) rewards the student who understands that the $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ answer is a consequence of the energy bookkeeping rather than a lucky guess, and it is marked so that guessing $0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ without the comparison does not score full marks.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.4 Resonance positions in a closed tube, and the end correction that cancels
questions.question:
A tuning fork of frequency $f = 512\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is held over the open upper end of a vertical tube closed at the lower end by a movable piston. The air column is adjusted until resonance is heard, and the three shortest resonating lengths are found to be $L_{1} = 0.160\ \mathrm{m}$, $L_{2} = 0.500\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L_{3} = 0.840\ \mathrm{m}$.

(a)

Determine the wavelength of the sound in the tube, explaining why the three lengths are used in the way you choose rather than $L_{1}$ alone.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the speed of sound in the air column.

[3]

(c)

Determine the end correction of the tube, and state its value to two significant figures.

[2]

(d)

Explain why using $L_{1}$ alone would give an incorrect speed of sound, and state by what percentage the value would be wrong.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) A tube closed at one end resonates when its length is an odd number of quarter wavelengths, but the antinode at the open end lies a small distance $e$ beyond the tube, so
$$L_{n} = (2n-1)\frac{\lambda}{4} - e$$

Subtracting consecutive lengths removes $e$ exactly (M1):
$$L_{2} - L_{1} = \frac{\lambda}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = 2(L_{2} - L_{1}) = 2(0.500 - 0.160) = 0.680\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1(A1)}$$

Using $L_{1}$ alone would require knowing $e$, which is not given; the difference is used precisely because the unknown cancels.

(b) (M1)(A1)
$$v = f\lambda = 512 \times 0.680 = 348\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

to three significant figures (A1).

(c) From the first resonance (M1):
$$e = \frac{\lambda}{4} - L_{1} = \frac{0.680}{4} - 0.160 = 0.170 - 0.160 = 0.010\ \mathrm{m} \tag{A1}$$

The end correction is $0.010\ \mathrm{m}$, or $10\ \mathrm{mm}$, of the order of the tube radius.

The data are consistent: $\dfrac{3\lambda}{4} - e = 0.510 - 0.010 = 0.500\ \mathrm{m} = L_{2}$ and $\dfrac{5\lambda}{4} - e = 0.850 - 0.010 = 0.840\ \mathrm{m} = L_{3}$, both exact.

(d) Using $L_{1}$ alone assumes the antinode is exactly at the open end, so it takes $\lambda = 4L_{1} = 0.640\ \mathrm{m}$ (M1). Then
$$v = 512 \times 0.640 = 328\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \tag{A1}$$

The percentage error is
$$\frac{348.16 - 327.68}{348.16} \times 100 = 3.0\ \%$$

too low. The error is entirely in the wavelength, because the neglected end correction shortens the apparent quarter wavelength by $0.010\ \mathrm{m}$ out of $0.170\ \mathrm{m}$, which is $5.9\ \%$ (A1).

The strongest evidence that the model is the right one is that two fitted numbers, the wavelength and the end correction, reproduce all three measured resonance lengths exactly. Three independent measurements have been reduced to two parameters with nothing left over, which a wrong model would not achieve. That is also why the data were given as three lengths rather than one: a single length can always be explained by a single fitted quantity, but it cannot be checked.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on a single structural fact about closed tubes: the three resonance lengths are equally spaced, because successive resonances differ by half a wavelength, and the end correction is the same for each. That means the unknown appears with the same sign and the same value in every measurement, so subtracting two of them annihilates it. This is the standard experimental trick for measuring a wavelength in a closed tube, and it is the reason the data contain three lengths rather than one.

The trap is the natural first move. Given a frequency and a resonance length, the tempting route is $\lambda = 4L_{1}$ and then $v = f\lambda$, which uses one number and requires no thought about the open end. It is also wrong, because the antinode is not at the open end but slightly outside it: the air just beyond the tube also moves. With these numbers the omission produces $328\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ against $348\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, a discrepancy of three per cent that is larger than the year-to-year spread of the accepted value, so it matters.

Part (d) asks for the size of the error rather than just its existence, which forces the student to actually compute the wrong answer and compare it. That comparison is what makes the item diagnostic: a student who writes "it would be slightly wrong" has not understood that the correction is a fixed length, and a fixed length is a much larger fraction of the shortest resonance than of the longest. The check at the end of part (c), reproducing both $L_{2}$ and $L_{3}$ from the fitted $\lambda$ and $e$, is there so that the student can see the model is exactly consistent with the data rather than approximately so.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.4 Two determinations of the same speed by standing waves in a tube, where the neglected end correction is worth more than either measurement's uncertainty
questions.question:
The two determinations of the speed of sound, and the readings each student took, are described in the stimulus and its table. Answer all parts using those readings.

(a)

Calculate the wavelength of the sound in Student A's tube from the spacing of his three resonance positions, and hence calculate his value for the speed of sound.

[3]

(b)

Determine the end correction of the tube from Student A's first resonance position, and explain why the spacing of the positions cannot give it.

[2]

(c)

One of Student B's three frequencies is inconsistent with the others. Identify it, justify your choice, determine Student B's value for the speed of sound from the remaining two readings, and explain why his value is systematically lower than Student A's.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate which of the two determinations of the speed of sound should be quoted, comparing the effect of random uncertainty on each with the effect of the systematic term.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Successive resonances in a tube closed at one end occur at $L = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} - e$, $\dfrac{3\lambda}{4} - e$, $\dfrac{5\lambda}{4} - e$, so consecutive positions differ by $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ (M1).

$$0.494 - 0.161 = 0.333\ \mathrm{m}, \qquad 0.827 - 0.494 = 0.333\ \mathrm{m} \;\; (A1).$$
$$\lambda = 2 \times 0.333 = 0.666\ \mathrm{m}, \qquad v = f\lambda = 512 \times 0.666 = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (A1).$$
To three significant figures, $v = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The two spacings agree to the nearest millimetre, so the random uncertainty on $\lambda$ is about $\dfrac{0.002}{0.333} = 0.6\%$ at worst, and on $v$ it is smaller still.

(b) The first resonance occurs where $L + e = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$ (M1), so
$$e = \frac{\lambda}{4} - L_{1} = 0.1665 - 0.161 = 0.0055\ \mathrm{m} = 5.5\ \mathrm{mm} \;\; (A1).$$

The spacing cannot give it because $e$ is common to every resonance position. Subtracting one position from the next removes $e$ entirely: $L_{2} - L_{1} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ whatever the end correction is. The spacing therefore determines $\lambda$ but carries no information about $e$, and it is only by referring a position to the *beginning* of the pattern -- which requires knowing that the first resonance is a quarter wavelength -- that $e$ can be extracted. For this tube the correction is $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, which is about $0.3$ of the $18\ \mathrm{mm}$ radius, as expected for a tube of this diameter.

(c) Two of the three frequencies should differ by twice the fundamental. Using the first and third,
$$\frac{843 - 169}{4} = \frac{674}{4} = 168.5\ \mathrm{Hz} \;\; (M1),$$
so the middle resonance should be at $169 + 2(168.5) = 506\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is the inconsistent reading (A1). A $4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ error is four times the generator's $1\ \mathrm{Hz}$ resolution.

Student B used $v = 4f_{0}L$ with the first resonance at the fundamental:
$$v = 4 \times 168.5 \times 0.500 = 337\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (A1).$$

His value is lower by $341 - 337 = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is $1.2\%$. The cause is that he omitted the end correction. The correct relation is $v = 4f_{0}(L + e)$, so
$$v = 4 \times 168.5 \times (0.500 + 0.0055) = 341\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},$$
which is Student A's value to three significant figures. Omitting $e$ is not a random error: it always makes the effective length too short, so the inferred speed is always too low, and the size of the effect is fixed by the tube rather than by the care taken in reading the dial. The anomaly at $510\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is a separate matter -- probably the reading was taken while the generator's display was still settling -- and it does not affect the value used, because the fundamental was obtained from the first and third readings.

(d) Student A's value should be quoted (A1).

His random uncertainty is dominated by the $\pm 1\ \mathrm{mm}$ reading of the positions, which over a $333\ \mathrm{mm}$ spacing is $0.3\%$, and the tuning fork's frequency is a specification held to better than $0.1\%$. His systematic term is handled rather than ignored: the end correction is obtained from the data and applied, so what remains is the assumption that $e$ is the same at every resonance, which is good to well under a millimetre.

Student B's random uncertainties are comparable -- $1\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in $169\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is $0.6\%$ -- but he carries an unaddressed systematic term of $1.1\%$ from the omitted end correction, and a systematic term is not reduced by repeating the measurement. His result is therefore both lower than Student A's and less trustworthy, and the fact that correcting $e$ brings his value onto Student A's is itself evidence that the correction is the right explanation rather than an arbitrary adjustment (A1).
questions.explanation:
Two students measure one number and get $341$ and $337$. The reflex is to ask which is careless, and the answer here is neither. The gap is $1.2\%$, and every random uncertainty in the experiment is smaller than that: the positions are read to a millimetre over a third of a metre, and the frequencies to a hertz in a hundred and seventy. Something systematic is at work, and the item is built so that it can be identified rather than guessed at.

The systematic term is the end correction. A tube closed at one end has an antinode slightly outside the open end, so the acoustically effective length is $L + e$ with $e$ roughly a third of the radius -- here $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ for an $18\ \mathrm{mm}$ radius. Student A's method extracts it because he refers an absolute position to the quarter-wavelength condition. Student B's method cannot, because he never uses a position at all: he treats the tube length as the whole of the acoustically effective length and computes $4fL$. The error is one-sided and always in the same direction, and $4fL$ with $f = 168.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$ gives $337$ against the $341$ that $4f(L+e)$ gives. The agreement after correction is the point of part (d): a candidate who finds the removal of $e$ turning $337$ into $341$ has located the cause, not merely adjusted a number.

The seeded anomaly is a different lesson. The three frequencies $169$, $510$ and $843$ should be equally spaced in steps of twice the fundamental, and $169$ to $843$ is four steps of $168.5$, which puts the middle reading at $506$ and not $510$. The reading is $4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ out -- four times the dial's resolution -- and the correct response is to identify it, exclude it and say what probably happened. Averaging the three frequencies to "fix" the anomaly is the classic wrong turn, because the average of a consistent pair and an inconsistent third is inconsistent with all three.

The two lessons are connected and it is worth saying how. A discrepancy that is larger than the uncertainties and always in the same direction is a systematic effect and needs a mechanism; a single reading that violates a pattern the others obey is an anomaly and needs to be excluded. Confusing the two -- treating the systematic offset as noise, or treating the anomaly as a discovery -- produces either a wrong answer or a wrong explanation, and the question is arranged so that both mistakes are available.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme D: Fields
questions.subtopic: D.3 A cyclotron, whose exit energy is fixed by the flux density and the radius of the dees and not by the accelerating potential difference, so that raising the voltage changes the number of revolutions rather than the energy
questions.question:
A cyclotron is to be used to accelerate protons, and its operating frequency and exit energy must be established. Show that the time for a proton to complete one full circular path inside the dees is $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ and that this time does not depend on the proton's speed, and calculate the frequency the alternating potential difference must have. Then determine the maximum speed the protons can reach, calculate the maximum kinetic energy and the number of revolutions a proton makes, and explain what does and does not raise the maximum energy.

(a)

Show that the time $T$ taken by a proton to complete one full circular path inside the dees is $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$, and that this time is independent of the proton's speed. Calculate $T$ for the fields given, and hence state the frequency at which the alternating potential difference must be applied.

[3]

(b)

Determine the maximum speed of a proton as it leaves the cyclotron, and express this speed as a fraction of the speed of light.

[2]

(c)

Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the protons in joules and in MeV, and hence calculate the number of revolutions a proton makes before it leaves the cyclotron.

[3]

(d)

Explain why raising the peak value of the alternating potential difference does not increase the maximum kinetic energy of the protons, and state one change to the apparatus that would increase it.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Inside a dee the only force is the magnetic force, and it acts at right angles to the velocity, so it supplies the centripetal force (D.3):
$$qvB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad r = \frac{mv}{qB}.$$
The circumference of the circular path is $2\pi r$, and the proton covers it at speed $v$, so
$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi}{v} \cdot \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB} \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
The speed cancels. That is the whole reason the machine works: a faster proton has a larger radius but covers the larger circumference in the same time, so a single fixed frequency accelerates the proton all the way out (A1).

Numerically,
$$T = \frac{2\pi \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2} = 5.47 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s},$$
so the alternating potential difference must be supplied at
$$f = \frac{1}{T} = 1.83 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Hz} \approx 18\ \mathrm{MHz}.$$
The proton crosses the gap twice in each revolution, so the potential difference must complete one full cycle in the same time $T$; the required frequency is therefore $f = qB/2\pi m$, about $18\ \mathrm{MHz}$.

(b) The protons leave when the radius of the path has grown to the radius of the dees, $r = R$ (D.3). From $r = mv/qB$,
$$v_{\max} = \frac{qBR}{m} = \frac{1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2 \times 0.35}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = 4.02 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
As a fraction of the speed of light this is
$$\frac{v_{\max}}{c} = \frac{4.02 \times 10^{7}}{3.00 \times 10^{8}} = 0.134,$$
about thirteen per cent of $c$. That justifies the non-relativistic treatment, since the mass of a proton at $0.134c$ is only about $0.9\%$ greater than its rest mass.

(c) The maximum kinetic energy follows from the speed in part (b):
$$E_{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times (4.02 \times 10^{7})^{2} = 1.35 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (A1).$$
Equivalently, and more directly from the geometry,
$$E_{k} = \frac{q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}}{2m} = \frac{(1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.2 \times 0.35)^{2}}{2 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = 1.35 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}.$$
In electronvolts,
$$E_{k} = \frac{1.35 \times 10^{-12}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 8.4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV} = 8.4\ \mathrm{MeV} \;\; (A1).$$

A proton gains energy $qV$ each time it crosses the gap, and it crosses the gap twice per revolution, so it gains $2qV = 2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 5.0 \times 10^{4} = 1.60 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{J}$ per revolution. The number of revolutions is therefore
$$N = \frac{1.35 \times 10^{-12}}{1.60 \times 10^{-14}} = 84.5,$$
that is about $85$ revolutions (A1). The protons cross the gap about $169$ times. Since the period does not change as the protons speed up, the total acceleration time is simply $N T = 84.5 \times 5.47 \times 10^{-8} \approx 4.6\ \mu\mathrm{s}$.

(d) The protons leave when the radius has grown to the fixed radius of the dees, and the speed at that moment is fixed by the fields through $v = qBR/m$ (D.3). Because $R$, $B$, $m$ and $q$ are all properties of the apparatus or the particle, the exit speed is fixed too, and so is the exit energy $\tfrac{1}{2}q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}/m$ (A1).

The voltage never appears in that expression. What the voltage sets is the *energy per crossing*, $qV$, and so the number of crossings needed, $E_{k}/qV$. Raising the voltage from $50\ \mathrm{kV}$ to $100\ \mathrm{kV}$ would double the energy gained at each crossing and halve the number of revolutions, from about $85$ to about $42$, leaving the energy the protons leave with unchanged (A1). The product of the two is the same because both are constrained by the same geometry: the protons have to reach the same radius, and reaching it requires the same total energy however it was delivered.

To raise the maximum energy, the ceiling itself has to be moved. Since $E_{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}/m$, a larger flux density $B$ or a larger dee radius $R$ would do it; both appear squared, so a $10\%$ increase in either raises the maximum energy by about $21\%$ (A1). Increasing $B$ is the cheaper change in practice because it does not require a larger magnet, but it runs into the relativistic limit: once $v$ is an appreciable fraction of $c$, the proton's mass increases and its period $T = 2\pi m/qB$ is no longer constant, so the fixed frequency falls out of step with the protons and the acceleration stalls. A cyclotron can only be extended in $B$ or $R$ until that happens, which is why higher-energy machines use a varying frequency.
questions.explanation:
The interesting thing about a cyclotron is not the force arithmetic, which is two lines long, but the fact that the machine works at all. A proton that is moving faster should take longer to go round a bigger circle; the reason it does not is that the radius and the speed grow together, so the period is unchanged. Every cyclotron question that is worth asking is a consequence of that cancellation, and this item asks for it first because the rest of the question only makes sense once it is understood.

Part (a) is the derivation. From $qvB = mv^2/r$ the radius is $mv/qB$, the circumference is proportional to $v$, and the time to cover it does not depend on $v$ at all. That is what allows a single fixed-frequency supply to serve the whole acceleration: the protons come round in step with the voltage no matter how fast they are going. A student who has memorised $T = 2\pi m/qB$ can quote it; the part asks for the cancellation explicitly.

Part (c) is where the difficulty sits. The tempting route is to say that a proton gains $qV$ per crossing and therefore ends up with $qV$ times the number of crossings, and then to invent a number of crossings from the observation that the protons leave after roughly eighty-five turns. That reasoning is circular and gets the answer right only by accident. The honest route is to note that the protons leave when $r = R$, which fixes $v$, which fixes the energy, and then to work out the number of revolutions as a consequence. The two routes give the same number, which is exactly why the error survives: the answer is right and the mechanism is wrong.

Part (d) is the part that separates the two. The voltage is the only thing putting energy in, and yet it cannot change what the protons leave with. What it changes is how many bites at the apple are needed. Doubling the voltage halves the number of revolutions and leaves the exit energy alone. The exit energy is a property of the apparatus -- the magnet and the size of the dees -- and to change it one of those has to change. This is a genuinely useful thing to know about particle accelerators, and it is the reason that the largest cyclotrons were abandoned in favour of machines that vary the frequency or the field.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.2 An impulse obtained as the area under a force-time record whose sampling interval changed part-way through, so that the area depends on reading the time column rather than assuming a constant step
questions.question:
The force sensor's record of the collision, the trolley's mass and the light gate's reading of the approach speed are given in the stimulus and its table. Answer all parts using those readings.

(a)

State the two different sampling intervals present in the record and the number of intervals of each kind, and explain why a trapezium rule applied to this table must use the time differences as given.

[2]

(b)

Determine the impulse delivered to the trolley, using the trapezium rule on the recorded pairs of values and stating the unit of your answer.

[3]

(c)

Determine the trolley's speed immediately after the collision, and determine the value a candidate who assumed a constant $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ interval would obtain for the impulse and for that speed.

[3]

(d)

Suggest what should have been recorded at the time to make this record analysable without ambiguity, and state how the uncertainty in the impulse could best be estimated from the data available.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) Reading the time column: the first four intervals are $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ each, the intervals $30 \to 35 \to 40$ are $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ each, and the last two are $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ (A1). So there are four intervals of $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ ($0$-$10$, $10$-$20$, $20$-$30$, $40$-$50$, $50$-$60$ is five) -- counting them explicitly: $0$-$10$, $10$-$20$, $20$-$30$, $40$-$50$ and $50$-$60$ are five intervals of $10\ \mathrm{ms}$, and $30$-$35$, $35$-$40$ are two intervals of $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ (A1). Total record length $60\ \mathrm{ms}$.

The trapezium rule approximates $\int F\,dt$ by $\sum \tfrac{1}{2}(F_{i} + F_{i+1})\Delta t_{i}$, so each pair of forces must be weighted by the time difference that actually separates them. The force is not a function of sample number; it is a function of time, and the samples are not equally spaced in time. Using a single step $\Delta t = 10\ \mathrm{ms}$ for all seven intervals would assign the same weight to a $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ interval as to a $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ one, which inflates the area near the peak where the sampling was fastest.

(b) Apply the trapezium rule interval by interval (M1):
$$\begin{aligned}
0\text{-}10: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(0.0 + 4.2)(10) = 21.0 \\
10\text{-}20: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(4.2 + 9.8)(10) = 70.0 \\
20\text{-}30: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8 + 15.6)(10) = 127.0 \\
30\text{-}35: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(15.6 + 19.4)(5) = 87.5 \\
35\text{-}40: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(19.4 + 18.2)(5) = 94.0 \\
40\text{-}50: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(18.2 + 11.0)(10) = 146.0 \\
50\text{-}60: &\ \tfrac{1}{2}(11.0 + 3.4)(10) = 72.0
\end{aligned}$$
The sum is in $\mathrm{N\,ms}$, so
$$\sum = 21.0 + 70.0 + 127.0 + 87.5 + 94.0 + 146.0 + 72.0 = 617.5\ \mathrm{N\,ms} \;\; (A1).$$
$$J = 617.5 \times 10^{-3} = 0.6175\ \mathrm{N\,s} \approx 0.62\ \mathrm{N\,s} \;\; (A1).$$
The unit is the newton second, $\mathrm{N\,s}$, equivalently $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

(c) The impulse equals the change in momentum, $J = \Delta p = m(v - u)$ with $u = +0.450\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (M1):
$$v = u + \frac{J}{m} = 0.450 + \frac{0.6175}{0.850} = 0.450 + 0.7265 = 1.18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \;\; (A1).$$

A candidate who assumes a constant $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ interval weights the two short intervals as though they were twice as long:
$$\sum = 21.0 + 70.0 + 127.0 + 175.0 + 188.0 + 146.0 + 72.0 = 799.0\ \mathrm{N\,ms},$$
so $J = 0.799\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and $v = 0.450 + \dfrac{0.799}{0.850} = 1.39\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (A1).

The error is $\dfrac{799.0 - 617.5}{617.5} = 29\%$ in the impulse and $($1.39 - 1.18$)/$1.18$ = 18\%$ in the speed. It arises entirely from the two $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ intervals at the peak, where the force is largest and where doubling the assumed width adds the most area.

(d) The sampling interval should have been fixed by the operator and recorded with the data, together with a note of any change; on an automatic rate the interval is a property of the logger rather than of the experiment, and a record whose abscissa is not documented cannot be integrated unambiguously. A second clock channel, or a fixed rate with the interval written in the log, would settle it (A1).

Given the record as it stands, the honest estimate of the uncertainty in the impulse comes from the force resolution: each sample carries $\pm 0.2\ \mathrm{N}$, and the trapezium rule weights each sample by half the sum of the two intervals that touch it, namely $\tfrac{1}{2}(10 + 10) = 10\ \mathrm{ms}$ for an interior sample at a $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ step and $\tfrac{1}{2}(10 + 5) = 7.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ for one at the junction. Adding the contributions in quadrature gives a few tenths of a per cent of the total, so the resolution is not the limiting factor -- the sampling interval is (A1). The duration itself has no quoted uncertainty, so a defensible statement is that the impulse is known to about $1\%$ from the record and to whatever the undocumented interval change contributes on top.
questions.explanation:
This question is about a collision and it is not really about collisions. The physics is one line -- impulse is the area under a force-time graph and equals the change in momentum -- and the work is in noticing what the data actually are.

The record has eight samples and seven intervals, and the intervals are not equal: two of them are $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ where the rest are $10\ \mathrm{ms}$. This is not a hypothetical hazard. Loggers with an automatic rate setting really do change interval mid-record, usually to capture detail where the signal is changing fastest, which is exactly where the force is largest and where the area is most sensitive to the width assumed. The two short intervals carry a total area of $181.5\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$; treating them as $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ each makes that $350\ \mathrm{N\,ms}$, and the impulse comes out $29\%$ too large.

The reason this is a trap worth setting is that nothing about the numbers looks wrong. The forces are plausible and rise and fall smoothly, the times are in increasing order, and the table is not missing any rows. A candidate who reads the force column and takes the step for granted is doing arithmetic on an assumed dataset rather than the one in front of them, and the mark scheme is arranged so that this candidate scores the method mark in (b) and then sees, in (c), exactly what the assumption cost. Showing the wrong value inside the question rather than merely penalising it is deliberate: the point is that $1.39$ and $1.18$ are both "reasonable" numbers for a trolley to rebound with, and only the time column distinguishes them.

Part (d) is where the item finishes rather than where it tails off. The uncertainty in the impulse is *not* dominated by the sensor's resolution -- that contributes a few tenths of a per cent -- but by whether the abscissa can be trusted at all, which is a recording decision made before the collision happened. A candidate who produces a careful quadrature sum from the resolution and reports a comfortable $0.2\%$ has answered a question that the data do not support, and saying so is the judgement this part rewards.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.4 The fuel-cycle arithmetic of a fission reactor carried through from the energy per fission to the mass of enriched uranium per year, and the sensitivity of the comparison with coal to the assumptions behind it
questions.question:
A pressurised water reactor operates with a thermal power output of $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ and converts this to electrical energy with an efficiency of $33\%$. Each fission of a $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nucleus releases $202\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The reactor is refuelled with uranium enriched to $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ by mass, and the remainder is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$, which does not undergo fission in this reactor. Use $N_{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ and one year $= 3.15 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(a)

Show that the fission of all the nuclei in $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ would release about $8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$ of energy.

[2]

(b)

Determine the mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ that undergoes fission in one year of continuous operation at the stated output.

[3]

(c)

Determine the mass of enriched uranium that must be loaded each year to supply that quantity of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$, and determine the mass of coal that would be needed each year to generate the same electrical energy in a station burning coal of energy content $2.4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ at an efficiency of $38\%$.

[2]

(d)

Evaluate the comparison in part (c) as a measure of the environmental advantage of the reactor, referring to at least two assumptions that the comparison makes.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The number of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nuclei in $1.00\ \mathrm{kg}$ (M1):
$$N = \frac{1.00}{235 \times 10^{-3}}\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} = \frac{1000}{235} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 2.56 \times 10^{24}.$$

The energy released per fission is
$$202\ \mathrm{MeV} = 202 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.23 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J},$$
so
$$E = 2.56 \times 10^{24} \times 3.23 \times 10^{-11} = 8.28 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J} \approx 8.3 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (A1).$$

(b) The electrical output is
$$P_{e} = 0.33 \times 3.0 \times 10^{9} = 9.9 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{W} \;\; (M1).$$
In one year the electrical energy delivered is
$$E_{e} = 9.9 \times 10^{8} \times 3.15 \times 10^{7} = 3.12 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{J} \;\; (M1).$$
All of this comes from fission, so the mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ fissioned is
$$m = \frac{3.12 \times 10^{16}}{8.28 \times 10^{13}} = 377\ \mathrm{kg} \;\; (A1).$$

It is worth noting that the efficiency cancels out of nothing here: the thermal power of $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ is what the fuel must supply, so an alternative route is to use $3.0 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{W}$ directly and compute $m = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{9} \times 3.15 \times 10^{7}}{8.28 \times 10^{13}} = 1141\ \mathrm{kg}$ of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ -- but that is the mass fissioned to supply the *thermal* output, and the electrical output is what the question asks about. Working in electrical energy throughout, as above, avoids the confusion.

(c) The $377\ \mathrm{kg}$ is $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ alone. Since the fuel contains only $4.0\%$ $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ by mass (M1):
$$m_{\text{fuel}} = \frac{377}{0.040} = 9.4 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 9.4\ \mathrm{tonnes} \;\; (A1).$$
So just under ten tonnes of enriched uranium per year, of which about $9.0\ \mathrm{t}$ is $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ that does not fission.

For coal, the energy must be supplied as chemical energy and the conversion is less efficient:
